natural.es: Las funciones trigonométricas son las funciones seno, coseno, tangente, cotangente, secante y cosecante. Se definen en términos de las razones de los lados de un triángulo rectángulo o, de manera más general, usando el círculo unitario.

definition.trigonometric-function.notes: Stewart reviews trigonometric functions in section 1.2 as part of the catalog of essential functions, assuming prior knowledge from precalculus.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: Let f be a mapping of a metric space X into a metric space Y. We say that f is uniformly continuous on X if for every ε > 0 there exists δ > 0 such that d_Y(f(p), f(q)) < ε for all p and q in X for which d_X(p, q) < δ.

definition.uniform-continuity.notes: Rudin Definition 4.18. Key distinction from pointwise continuity: the same δ works for all points simultaneously. Every uniformly continuous function is continuous, but not conversely in general.

natural.en: If {Eα} is a family of sets indexed by A, the union ⋃α Eα is the set of all x belonging to at least one Eα. The intersection ⋂α Eα is the set of all x belonging to every Eα. If A ∩ B is not empty, A and B intersect; otherwise they are disjoint.

definition.union-intersection.notes: Definition 2.9 from Rudin. Generalizes union and intersection to arbitrary indexed families.

title.en: Union and Intersection of Families of Sets

natural.en: The unit step function I is defined by I(x) = 0 if x <= 0 and I(x) = 1 if x > 0.

Suppose S is an ordered set, and E ⊂ S. If there exists a β ∈ S such that x ≤ β for every x ∈ E, we say that E is bounded above, and call β an upper bound of E. Lower bounds are defined in the same way (with ≥ in place of ≤).

definition.upper-bound.notes: Rudin 1.7. Dual notion of lower bound is implicit.

natural.en: Let {s_n} be a sequence of real numbers. Let E be the set of numbers x (in the extended real number system) such that s_{n_k} → x for some subsequence {s_{n_k}}. Then sup E is called the upper limit (or limit superior) of {s_n}, and inf E is called the lower limit (or limit inferior) of {s_n}.

definition.upper-lower-limits.notes: Definition 3.16 from Rudin's Principles of Mathematical Analysis.

natural.en: Let f_1, ..., f_k be real functions on [a, b], and let f = (f_1, ..., f_k) be the corresponding mapping into R^k. If alpha increases monotonically on [a, b], we say f in R(alpha) means f_j in R(alpha) for j = 1, ..., k. In that case, integral f d alpha = (integral f_1 d alpha, ..., integral f_k d alpha).

The vertical line x = a is called a vertical asymptote of the curve y = f(x) if at least one of the following holds: lim(x→a) f(x) = ∞, lim(x→a) f(x) = -∞, lim(x→a⁺) f(x) = ∞, lim(x→a⁺) f(x) = -∞, lim(x→a⁻) f(x) = ∞, lim(x→a⁻) f(x) = -∞.
natural.es: La recta vertical x = a se llama asíntota vertical de la curva y = f(x) si se cumple al menos una de las siguientes condiciones: lim(x→a) f(x) = ∞, lim(x→a) f(x) = -∞, lim(x→a⁺) f(x) = ∞, lim(x→a⁺) f(x) = -∞, lim(x→a⁻) f(x) = ∞, lim(x→a⁻) f(x) = -∞.

definition.vertical-shift.latex: y = f(x) + c \quad (c > 0 \text{: arriba}), \quad y = f(x) - c \quad (c > 0 \text{: abajo})

natural.en: If c > 0, the graph of y = f(x) + c is obtained by shifting the graph of y = f(x) upward c units. The graph of y = f(x) - c is obtained by shifting the graph downward c units.
natural.es: Si c > 0, la gráfica de y = f(x) + c se obtiene desplazando la gráfica de y = f(x) hacia arriba c unidades. La gráfica de y = f(x) - c se obtiene desplazando la gráfica hacia abajo c unidades.

definition.vertical-shift.notes: Part of the catalog of transformations in section 1.3.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: If c > 1, the graph of y = cf(x) is obtained by stretching the graph of y = f(x) vertically by a factor of c. If 0 < c < 1, the graph is compressed vertically by a factor of c.
natural.es: Si c > 1, la gráfica de y = cf(x) se obtiene estirando la gráfica de y = f(x) verticalmente por un factor de c. Si 0 < c < 1, la gráfica se comprime verticalmente por un factor de c.

definition.vertical-stretch-compression.notes: Part of the catalog of transformations in section 1.3.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: Let S be a solid that lies between x = a and x = b. If the cross-sectional area of S in the plane P_x, perpendicular to the x-axis, is A(x), where A is a continuous function, then the volume of S is V = ∫_a^b A(x) dx.
natural.es: Sea S un sólido que se extiende desde x = a hasta x = b. Si la sección transversal de S en el plano P_x, perpendicular al eje x, tiene área A(x), donde A es una función continua, entonces el volumen de S es V = ∫_a^b A(x) dx.

definition.volume-by-cross-sections.notes: The general volume formula obtained by slicing the solid into thin slabs of thickness Δx. The cross-sectional area A(x) must be a known, continuous function. Disk and washer methods are special cases of this definition.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: If the region under the curve y = f(x) from a to b (with 0 ≤ a < b) is rotated about the y-axis, the volume of the resulting solid of revolution is V = ∫_a^b 2πx f(x) dx.
natural.es: Si la región bajo la curva y = f(x) desde a hasta b (con 0 ≤ a < b) se hace girar alrededor del eje y, el volumen del sólido de revolución resultante es V = ∫_a^b 2πx f(x) dx.

definition.volume-by-cylindrical-shells.notes: The shell method provides an alternative to the disk/washer method when rotation is about an axis parallel to the slicing variable. Each cylindrical shell has radius x, height f(x), and thickness dx, giving a shell volume of 2πx f(x) dx.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: If the region under the curve y = f(x) from a to b is rotated about the x-axis, the volume of the resulting solid of revolution is V = ∫_a^b π[f(x)]² dx. If the region is between y = f(x) and y = g(x) with f(x) ≥ g(x) ≥ 0, the washer method gives V = ∫_a^b π([f(x)]² - [g(x)]²) dx.
natural.es: Si la región bajo la curva y = f(x) desde a hasta b se hace girar alrededor del eje x, el volumen del sólido de revolución resultante es V = ∫_a^b π[f(x)]² dx. Si la región está entre y = f(x) y y = g(x) con f(x) ≥ g(x) ≥ 0, se usa el método de arandelas: V = ∫_a^b π([f(x)]² - [g(x)]²) dx.

definition.volume-of-revolution.notes: Special case of definition.volume-by-cross-sections where the cross-sections are circles (disks) or annuli (washers). The cross-sectional area is A(x) = π[f(x)]² for disks and A(x) = π([f(x)]² - [g(x)]²) for washers.

natural.en: If {Iₙ} is a sequence of intervals in R¹ with Iₙ ⊃ Iₙ₊₁, then ⋂Iₙ is nonempty.

lemma.nested-intervals.notes: Theorem 2.38 in Rudin. Uses the least upper bound property of R.

natural.en: If {Iₙ} is a sequence of k-cells with Iₙ ⊃ Iₙ₊₁, then ⋂Iₙ is nonempty.

lemma.nested-k-cells.notes: Theorem 2.39 in Rudin. Generalizes the nested intervals theorem to k dimensions.

proof.abel-cauchy-product.rudin.notes: Rudin states the result in Ch3 (Thm 3.51) but defers the proof to after Theorem 8.2, using continuity of power series. No assumption on absolute convergence needed.

proof.absolute-convergence-implies-conve.notes: Since 0 ≤ aₙ + |aₙ| ≤ 2|aₙ| and ∑ 2|aₙ| converges, the Comparison Test gives that ∑ (aₙ + |aₙ|) converges. Then ∑ aₙ = ∑ (aₙ + |aₙ|) - ∑ |aₙ| converges as the difference of two convergent series.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.absolute-convergence-rearrangement.notes: Choose N with tail < ε. Choose p so that 1,...,N all appear in first p terms of rearrangement. Then |s_n - s'_n| < ε for n>p.

proof.addition-cancellation.rudin.notes: (a) y = 0+y = (-x+x)+y = -x+(x+y) = -x+(x+z) = (-x+x)+z = 0+z = z. (b)-(d) follow from (a) by specialization.

proof.algebraic-limit-theorem.rudin.notes: Standard epsilon/2 arguments for sum; identity s_n t_n - st = (s_n-s)(t_n-t) + s(t_n-t) + t(s_n-s) for products; bound on |s_n| for quotients.

proof.alternating-series-test.stewart.notes: The even partial sums s₂ₙ form an increasing bounded sequence (since s₂ₙ₊₂ = s₂ₙ + (b₂ₙ₊₁ - b₂ₙ₊₂) ≥ s₂ₙ and s₂ₙ ≤ b₁). By the Monotonic Sequence Theorem, s₂ₙ → s. Since s₂ₙ₊₁ = s₂ₙ + b₂ₙ₊₁ → s + 0 = s, both subsequences converge to s, so sₙ → s.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.arc-length-formula.rudin.notes: Upper bound: |gamma(x_i) - gamma(x_{i-1})| = |integral gamma' dt| <= integral |gamma'| dt, so Lambda(P) <= integral |gamma'| dt. Lower bound: use uniform continuity of gamma' to show integral |gamma'| dt <= Lambda(P) + 2 epsilon (b-a) for fine enough P.

proof.archimedean-density.rudin.notes: (a) If A = {nx} were bounded above, α = sup A would satisfy α - x < mx for some m, giving α < (m+1)x ∈ A — contradiction. (b) Uses (a) twice to find integer m with m-1 ≤ nx < m, then nx < m ≤ 1 + nx < ny, so x < m/n < y.

proof.at-most-countable-union.rudin.notes: T is equivalent to a subset of the countable union.

proof.binary-sequences-uncountable.rudin.notes: Cantor's diagonal argument. Given any countable subset E = {s₁,s₂,...}, construct s differing from sₙ in the nth digit.

proof.bolzano-weierstrass.rudin.notes: Bounded E ⊂ k-cell I. I is compact. Apply Theorem 2.37.

proof.cancellation-equations.stewart.notes: Follows directly from the definition of inverse function. If f⁻¹(y) = x iff f(x) = y, then substituting y = f(x) gives f⁻¹(f(x)) = x, and substituting x = f⁻¹(y) gives f(f⁻¹(y)) = y.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.cauchy-condensation-test.rudin.notes: Show s_n ≤ t_k and 2s_n ≥ t_k by grouping terms in powers-of-2 blocks; both bounded or both unbounded.

proof.cauchy-criterion-series.rudin.notes: Restatement of Cauchy criterion for sequences applied to partial sums.

proof.cauchy-criterion.rudin.notes: (a) Triangle inequality. (b) Tail sets E̅_N are nested compact with diam→0; apply 3.10(b). (c) Cauchy in R^k ⟹ bounded ⟹ compact closure ⟹ apply (b).

proof.chain-rule.rudin.notes: Let y = f(x). Write f(t) - f(x) = (t - x)[f'(x) + u(t)] and g(s) - g(y) = (s - y)[g'(y) + v(s)] where u(t) → 0 and v(s) → 0. Setting s = f(t): (h(t) - h(x))/(t - x) = [g'(y) + v(s)][f'(x) + u(t)]. As t → x, s → y by continuity of f, giving h'(x) = g'(f(x))f'(x). This avoids the division-by-zero issue since it never divides by f(t) - f(x).

proof.chain-rule.stewart.notes: Define ε(Δu) so that Δy = f'(u)Δu + ε·Δu where ε→0 as Δu→0 (and ε(0) = 0). Then Δy/Δx = f'(u) · Δu/Δx + ε · Δu/Δx. As Δx→0, Δu→0 (by continuity of g), so ε→0, giving dy/dx = f'(u) · du/dx.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.change-of-base-formula.stewart.notes: Let y = logₐx. Then aʸ = x. Taking natural logarithm on both sides: y ln(a) = ln(x), so y = ln(x)/ln(a). This uses the power rule from the laws of logarithms applied to the natural logarithm.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.change-of-variable-integral.rudin.notes: Each partition P of [a,b] corresponds to Q of [A,B] via x_i = phi(y_i). Since phi is bijective, all partitions of [A,B] arise this way. The values of f on [x_{i-1}, x_i] equal those of g on [y_{i-1}, y_i], so U(Q,g,beta) = U(P,f,alpha) and L(Q,g,beta) = L(P,f,alpha).

proof.characterization-lim-sup.rudin.notes: Three cases: s*=+∞ (unbounded subsequence), s* real (closed set + bounded above), s*=-∞ (only -∞ in E). Uniqueness by contradiction.

proof.closed-intersect-compact.rudin.notes: F ∩ K is closed (intersection of two closed sets), and F ∩ K ⊂ K, so Theorem 2.35 applies.

proof.closed-subset-compact.rudin.notes: Adjoin Fᶜ (open) to any cover of F to get a cover of K. Extract finite subcover of K, remove Fᶜ.

proof.closure-properties.rudin.notes: (a) If p ∉ E̅, p has neighborhood not intersecting E, so E̅ᶜ is open. (b) E̅ = E iff E' ⊂ E. (c) Closed F ⊃ E implies F ⊃ E', hence F ⊃ E̅.

proof.compact-is-closed.rudin.notes: For p ∉ K, cover K by neighborhoods Wq disjoint from neighborhoods Vq of p. Finite subcover gives V ⊂ Kᶜ.

proof.compact-uniform-continuity.rudin.notes: For each p ∈ X, get φ(p) > 0 with d_Y(f(p),f(q)) < ε/2 when d_X(p,q) < φ(p). Let J(p) = B(p, φ(p)/2). Compactness gives finite subcover J(p₁),...,J(pₙ). Set δ = min{φ(pᵢ)}/2. For d_X(p,q) < δ, find pₘ with p ∈ J(pₘ), then both p and q are within φ(pₘ) of pₘ, so d_Y(f(p),f(q)) < ε by triangle inequality.

proof.compactness-relative.rudin.notes: Both directions use Theorem 2.30 to translate between open-in-X and open-relative-to-Y.

proof.comparison-lim-sup-inf.rudin.notes: Trivial from definitions; subsequential limits of {s_n} cannot exceed those of {t_n} when s_n ≤ t_n eventually.

proof.comparison-test-series.rudin.notes: |a_k| ≤ c_k gives Cauchy criterion for Σa_n from that of Σc_n. Divergence follows by contraposition.

proof.comparison-test-series.stewart.notes: Part (i): The partial sums of ∑ aₙ are bounded above by ∑ bₙ and increasing (since aₙ ≥ 0). By the Monotonic Sequence Theorem, they converge. Part (ii): follows from part (i) by contraposition.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.comparison-theorem-integrals.stewa.notes: Stewart gives an intuitive argument: since 0 ≤ g(x) ≤ f(x), the integral ∫_a^t g(x) dx ≤ ∫_a^t f(x) dx for all t ≥ a. If the larger integral converges, the smaller is bounded above and increasing, hence converges. The rigorous proof uses the monotone convergence property (completeness of reals), which is not explicitly proved.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.complex-absolute-value-properties..notes: (c) |zw|² = (ac-bd)² + (ad+bc)² = (a²+b²)(c²+d²) = |z|²|w|², then uniqueness of square roots. (e) Triangle inequality: |z+w|² = |z|² + 2Re(zw̄) + |w|² ≤ (|z|+|w|)² using |Re(zw̄)| ≤ |zw̄| = |z||w|.

proof.complex-field.rudin.notes: Direct verification of all field axioms (A1)-(A5), (M1)-(M5), and (D) for ordered pairs with the defined operations. The multiplicative inverse of (a,b) ≠ (0,0) is (a/(a²+b²), -b/(a²+b²)).

proof.composition-preserves-integrabilit.notes: Choose delta < epsilon with |phi(s) - phi(t)| < epsilon when |s-t| <= delta. Since f in R(alpha), find P with U(P,f,alpha) - L(P,f,alpha) < delta^2. Split indices into A (M_i - m_i < delta) and B (M_i - m_i >= delta). For A: M_i* - m_i* < epsilon. For B: sum Delta alpha_i < delta. Then U(P,h,alpha) - L(P,h,alpha) < epsilon[alpha(b) - alpha(a) + 2K].

proof.concavity-test.stewart.notes: f'' > 0 means f' is increasing by the increasing/decreasing test applied to f'. When f' is increasing, the tangent slope grows, so the curve lies above its tangent lines (concave up).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.conjugate-properties.rudin.notes: Parts (a), (b), (c) are direct computation. Part (d): if z = a+bi then zz̄ = a² + b², which is real and nonnegative, and zero only when a = b = 0.

proof.connected-subsets-of-r.rudin.notes: If z ∉ E with x < z < y (x,y ∈ E), split E = (E ∩ (-∞,z)) ∪ (E ∩ (z,∞)) — separated. Converse: if E not connected with A ∪ B = E, take x ∈ A, y ∈ B, z = sup(A ∩ [x,y]). By Theorem 2.28, z ∈ A̅, so z ∉ B, find z₁ ∉ E between z and y.

proof.constant-multiple-rule.stewart.notes: d/dx[cf(x)] = lim(h→0) [cf(x+h) - cf(x)]/h = c · lim(h→0) [f(x+h) - f(x)]/h = c f'(x) by the constant multiple law for limits.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.continuity-arithmetic-operations.r.notes: At isolated points, trivial. At limit points, follows from Theorems 4.4 and 4.6.

proof.continuity-closed-preimage.rudin.notes: A set is closed iff its complement is open, and f⁻¹(Eᶜ) = [f⁻¹(E)]ᶜ.

proof.continuity-components-rk.rudin.notes: Part (a): |f_j(x) - f_j(y)| ≤ |f(x) - f(y)| = (Σ|f_i(x)-f_i(y)|²)^{1/2}. Part (b): follows from (a) and Theorem 4.9.

proof.continuity-limit-point-equivalence.notes: Immediate from comparing Definitions 4.1 and 4.5. The only difference is that continuity uses d_X(x,p) < δ while the limit uses 0 < d_X(x,p) < δ; at a limit point, p ∈ E makes f(p) the relevant value.

proof.continuity-of-combinations.stewart.notes: Direct application of the limit laws to the definition of continuity. For example, lim(x→a) [f(x) + g(x)] = lim(x→a) f(x) + lim(x→a) g(x) = f(a) + g(a) = (f + g)(a).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.continuity-of-composition-metric.r.notes: Chain two ε-δ arguments: g continuous at f(p) gives η for ε; f continuous at p gives δ for η. Then d_X(x,p) < δ implies d_Z(h(x), h(p)) < ε.

proof.continuity-of-composition.stewart.notes: Given epsilon > 0, continuity of f at b gives delta_1 such that |y - b| < delta_1 implies |f(y) - f(b)| < epsilon. Since lim g(x) = b, there exists delta such that 0 < |x - a| < delta implies |g(x) - b| < delta_1. Combining gives the result.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.continuity-open-preimage.rudin.notes: Forward: f continuous, V open in Y. For p ∈ f⁻¹(V), f(p) ∈ V, so ∃ε with B(f(p),ε) ⊂ V. By continuity, ∃δ: d(x,p)<δ ⟹ f(x)∈V, so B(p,δ) ⊂ f⁻¹(V). Converse: given p, ε>0, let V = B(f(p),ε); V open, so f⁻¹(V) open, contains p, so ∃δ: B(p,δ) ⊂ f⁻¹(V).

proof.continuous-bijection-compact-inver.notes: Apply Thm 4.8 to f⁻¹: need f(V) open in Y for V open in X. Vᶜ closed in X, hence compact (Thm 2.35); f(Vᶜ) compact (Thm 4.14), hence closed (Thm 2.34). Since f is bijective, f(V) = [f(Vᶜ)]ᶜ, open.

proof.continuous-compact-to-rk-closed-bo.notes: Follows from Theorem 2.41: compact subsets of R^k are closed and bounded.

proof.continuous-image-compact.rudin.notes: Let {V_α} be an open cover of f(X). By Thm 4.8, each f⁻¹(V_α) is open. Since X is compact, finitely many cover X: X ⊂ f⁻¹(V_{α₁}) ∪ ... ∪ f⁻¹(V_{αₙ}). Then f(X) ⊂ V_{α₁} ∪ ... ∪ V_{αₙ}.

proof.continuous-image-connected.rudin.notes: By contradiction: if f(E) = A ∪ B separated, put G = E ∩ f⁻¹(A), H = E ∩ f⁻¹(B). Since f continuous and A̅ closed, f⁻¹(A̅) closed, G̅ ⊂ f⁻¹(A̅), so f(G̅) ⊂ A̅. Since f(H)=B and A̅∩B=∅, G̅∩H=∅. Similarly G∩H̅=∅. So G,H separated, contradicting E connected.

proof.continuous-integrable-stieltjes.ru.notes: Choose eta so that [alpha(b) - alpha(a)] eta < epsilon. By uniform continuity (Theorem 4.19), choose delta so that |f(x)-f(t)| < eta when |x-t| < delta. Any partition with Delta x_i < delta gives M_i - m_i <= eta, so U - L <= eta [alpha(b) - alpha(a)] < epsilon.

proof.convergence-in-rk.rudin.notes: Component inequality |α_{j,n} - α_j| ≤ |x_n - x| gives forward direction; sum of squares gives reverse.

proof.convergent-sequence-properties.rud.notes: Parts (a)-(d). Uses triangle inequality for uniqueness, picks r=max for boundedness, 1/n neighborhoods for limit point → sequence.

proof.countable-union-countable.rudin.notes: Diagonal arrangement of the double array. S is equivalent to a subset of J via Theorem 2.8.

proof.darboux-theorem.rudin.notes: Put g(t) = f(t) - lambda*t. Then g'(a) < 0, so g(t1) < g(a) for some t1 in (a,b), and g'(b) > 0, so g(t2) < g(b) for some t2 in (a,b). Hence g attains its minimum on [a,b] (Theorem 4.16, EVT) at some interior point x with a < x < b. By Theorem 5.8 (Fermat), g'(x) = 0, so f'(x) = lambda.

proof.de-morgan.rudin.notes: x ∈ (⋃Eα)ᶜ iff x ∉ Eα for any α iff x ∈ Eαᶜ for every α iff x ∈ ⋂Eαᶜ.

proof.derivative-arccos.stewart.notes: Let y = cos⁻¹ x, so cos y = x. Differentiate implicitly: -sin y · dy/dx = 1, so dy/dx = -1/sin y. Since sin y ≥ 0 on [0, π], sin y = √(1 - cos²y) = √(1 - x²).

proof.derivative-arcsin.stewart.notes: Let y = sin⁻¹ x, so sin y = x. Differentiate implicitly: cos y · dy/dx = 1, so dy/dx = 1/cos y. Since cos y ≥ 0 on [-π/2, π/2], cos y = √(1 - sin²y) = √(1 - x²).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-arctan.stewart.notes: Let y = tan⁻¹ x, so tan y = x. Differentiate implicitly: sec²y · dy/dx = 1, so dy/dx = 1/sec²y = cos²y. Since 1 + tan²y = sec²y, we get dy/dx = 1/(1 + tan²y) = 1/(1 + x²).

proof.derivative-cos.stewart.notes: cos(x+h) = cos x cos h - sin x sin h by the addition formula. Then [cos(x+h) - cos x]/h = cos x · (cos h - 1)/h - sin x · sin h/h. As h→0, this gives 0 - sin x = -sin x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-cot.stewart.notes: cot x = cos x / sin x. By the quotient rule: d/dx(cot x) = [(-sin x) sin x - cos x · cos x] / sin²x = -(sin²x + cos²x) / sin²x = -1/sin²x = -csc²x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-csc.stewart.notes: csc x = 1/sin x. By the quotient rule: d/dx(csc x) = [0 · sin x - 1 · cos x] / sin²x = -cos x / sin²x = -(1/sin x)(cos x/sin x) = -csc x cot x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-e-formula.stewart.notes: Since d/dx(ln x)|_{x=1} = 1, we have lim(h→0) [ln(1+h) - ln 1]/h = 1, i.e., lim(h→0) ln(1+h)/h = 1. So lim(h→0) ln(1+h)^{1/h} = 1, which gives (1+h)^{1/h} → e^1 = e.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-exponential.stewart.notes: d/dx(e^x) = lim(h→0) (e^{x+h} - e^x)/h = e^x · lim(h→0)(e^h - 1)/h = e^x · 1 = e^x, using the defining property of e.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-general-exponential.ste.notes: Write a^x = e^{x ln a}. By the chain rule: d/dx(e^{x ln a}) = e^{x ln a} · ln a = a^x ln a.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-ln-abs.stewart.notes: Case x > 0: ln|x| = ln x, so d/dx = 1/x. Case x < 0: ln|x| = ln(-x), so d/dx = (1/(-x))(-1) = 1/x by the chain rule. In both cases, d/dx(ln|x|) = 1/x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-ln.stewart.notes: Let y = ln x, so e^y = x. Differentiate implicitly: e^y · dy/dx = 1, so dy/dx = 1/e^y = 1/x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-log-base-a.stewart.notes: log_a x = ln x / ln a by the change of base formula. Then d/dx(log_a x) = (1/ln a) · d/dx(ln x) = (1/ln a)(1/x) = 1/(x ln a).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-no-simple-discontinuiti.notes: Immediate from Darboux's theorem (5.12). A simple (jump) discontinuity at c would mean the left and right limits of f' exist but differ, violating the intermediate value property established by 5.12.

proof.derivative-sec.stewart.notes: sec x = 1/cos x. By the quotient rule: d/dx(sec x) = [0 · cos x - 1 · (-sin x)] / cos²x = sin x / cos²x = (1/cos x)(sin x/cos x) = sec x tan x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-sin.stewart.notes: sin(x+h) = sin x cos h + cos x sin h by the addition formula. Then [sin(x+h) - sin x]/h = sin x · (cos h - 1)/h + cos x · sin h/h. As h→0, (cos h - 1)/h → 0 and sin h/h → 1, giving cos x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.derivative-sum-rule.rudin.notes: Rudin states "(a) is clear, by Theorem 4.4." The sum of difference quotients converges to the sum of derivatives by the limit sum law.

proof.derivative-tan.stewart.notes: tan x = sin x / cos x. By the quotient rule: d/dx(tan x) = [cos x · cos x - sin x · (-sin x)] / cos²x = (cos²x + sin²x) / cos²x = 1/cos²x = sec²x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.diameter-properties.rudin.notes: (a) diam E̅ = diam E by approximating closure points with E points. (b) Intersection nonempty by Thm 2.36; if more than one point, diam K > 0 contradicts diam K_n → 0.

proof.difference-rule.stewart.notes: f(x) - g(x) = f(x) + (-1)g(x). Apply the sum rule and the constant multiple rule with c = -1.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.differentiable-implies-continuous..notes: As t → x: f(t) - f(x) = [(f(t) - f(x))/(t - x)] · (t - x) → f'(x) · 0 = 0, by Theorem 4.4 (limit laws). Hence f is continuous at x.
Write f(x) - f(a) = [(f(x) - f(a))/(x - a)] · (x - a). Taking the limit as x → a: lim[f(x) - f(a)] = f'(a) · 0 = 0 by the product law. Therefore lim f(x) = f(a), so f is continuous at a.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.direct-substitution-property.stewa.notes: For polynomials: apply the sum, constant multiple, and power laws to each term. For rational functions: apply the quotient law with the polynomial result.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.dirichlet-test.rudin.notes: Apply summation by parts; |A_n|≤M and b_n↓0 give |Σa_n b_n| ≤ 2Mb_p ≤ 2Mb_N < ε.

proof.divergence-test.rudin.notes: Take m=n in the Cauchy criterion: |a_n| ≤ ε for n≥N, so a_n → 0.

proof.divergence-test.stewart.notes: Contrapositive of: if ∑ aₙ converges, then lim aₙ = 0. Proof: if ∑ aₙ = s, then sₙ → s and sₙ₋₁ → s. Since aₙ = sₙ - sₙ₋₁, we get aₙ → s - s = 0.

sources.author: James Stewart

proof.e-as-limit.rudin.notes: Binomial expansion of (1+1/n)^n shows t_n ≤ s_n, so lim sup t_n ≤ e. Lower bound by fixing m<n then letting n→∞, m→∞ gives lim inf t_n ≥ e.

proof.e-is-irrational.rudin.notes: If e=p/q, then 0 < q!(e - s_q) < 1/q. But q!·e integer, q!·s_q integer, so q!(e-s_q) is integer between 0 and 1, contradiction.

proof.equal-derivatives-differ-by-consta.notes: Let h = f - g. Then h'(x) = f'(x) - g'(x) = 0 for all x in (a,b). By the zero-derivative corollary, h is constant.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.euclidean-norm-properties.rudin.notes: (a)-(c) obvious. (d) is the Schwarz inequality applied to real components. (e) |x+y|² = |x|² + 2x·y + |y|² ≤ (|x|+|y|)² using (d). (f) follows from (e) with substitution x→x-y, y→y-z.

proof.existence-of-nth-roots.rudin.notes: Let E = {t > 0 : t^n < x}, y = sup E. Show y^n < x leads to (y+h)^n < x for small h (contradicting sup), and y^n > x leads to y-k being a smaller upper bound (contradicting least). Uses the identity b^n - a^n = (b-a)(b^{n-1} + ... + a^{n-1}).

proof.existence-of-reals.rudin.notes: Proof via Dedekind cuts (Appendix, Steps 1-9). A cut is a proper nonempty subset α of Q such that: (I) α ≠ Q, (II) if p ∈ α and q < p then q ∈ α, (III) α has no largest member. Addition and multiplication of cuts are defined and verified to satisfy field axioms. The LUB property follows from taking unions of cuts.

proof.extreme-value-theorem-compact-metr.notes: By Theorem 4.15, f(X) is a closed and bounded set of real numbers. By Theorem 2.28, a closed bounded set contains its sup and inf.

proof.extreme-value-theorem.stewart.notes: Stewart states the EVT without proof. A rigorous proof requires the completeness of the real numbers (the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem or the least upper bound property).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.fermat-theorem.rudin.notes: Choose delta so that f(t) <= f(x) for |t - x| < delta. For x - delta < t < x: (f(t) - f(x))/(t - x) >= 0, so f'(x) >= 0. For x < t < x + delta: (f(t) - f(x))/(t - x) <= 0, so f'(x) <= 0. Hence f'(x) = 0. Same argument applies for local minima.

proof.fermat-theorem.stewart.notes: Assume f has a local max at c and f'(c) exists. For h > 0 small, f(c+h) ≤ f(c), so [f(c+h)-f(c)]/h ≤ 0, giving f'(c) ≤ 0. For h < 0 small, [f(c+h)-f(c)]/h ≥ 0, giving f'(c) ≥ 0. Therefore f'(c) = 0. Analogous for local min.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.field-zero-product.rudin.notes: (a) 0x + 0x = (0+0)x = 0x, so 0x = 0 by 1.14(b). (b) If xy = 0 and x,y ≠ 0, then 1 = (1/x)(1/y)xy = 0, contradiction. (c) (-x)y + xy = (-x+x)y = 0y = 0, so (-x)y = -(xy) by 1.14(c). (d) (-x)(-y) = -[x(-y)] = -[-(xy)] = xy by (c) and 1.14(d).

proof.finite-intersection-compact.rudin.notes: Fix K₁, set Gα = Kαᶜ. If no point of K₁ is in every Kα, then {Gα} covers K₁. Finite subcover contradicts hypothesis.

proof.finite-set-no-limit-points.rudin.notes: A finite set cannot contain infinitely many points in any neighborhood.

proof.finitely-discontinuous-integrable..notes: Cover the finite discontinuity set E by disjoint intervals [u_j, v_j] with sum alpha(v_j) - alpha(u_j) < epsilon. The remaining set K is compact, so f is uniformly continuous on K. Build a partition that separates the discontinuity intervals, giving U - L <= [alpha(b) - alpha(a)] epsilon + 2M epsilon.

proof.first-derivative-test.stewart.notes: If f' > 0 on (c-δ, c) and f' < 0 on (c, c+δ), then f is increasing before c and decreasing after, so f(c) is a local max. Analogous for local min.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.ftc-part1.stewart.notes: g'(x) = lim(h→0) [g(x+h) - g(x)]/h = lim(h→0) (1/h)∫_x^{x+h} f(t)dt. By the comparison property, for h > 0: h·m(h) ≤ ∫_x^{x+h}f(t)dt ≤ h·M(h) where m(h) and M(h) are the min and max of f on [x, x+h]. Since f is continuous, both m(h) and M(h) → f(x) as h→0 by squeeze.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.ftc-part2.stewart.notes: Let g(x) = ∫_a^x f(t)dt. By FTC Part 1, g'(x) = f(x), so g is an antiderivative of f. If F is any other antiderivative, then F(x) = g(x) + C. So F(b) - F(a) = [g(b)+C] - [g(a)+C] = g(b) - g(a) = ∫_a^b f(t)dt - 0 = ∫_a^b f(t)dt.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.ftc-vector-valued.rudin.notes: Apply Theorem 6.21 to each component f_j with antiderivative F_j.

proof.fundamental-theorem-of-calculus.ru.notes: Choose partition P with U(P,f) - L(P,f) < epsilon. MVT gives t_i with F(x_i) - F(x_{i-1}) = f(t_i) Delta x_i. Thus sum f(t_i) Delta x_i = F(b) - F(a). By Theorem 6.7(c), |F(b) - F(a) - integral f| < epsilon.

proof.general-antiderivative.stewart.notes: If F and G are both antiderivatives of f, then F' = G' = f. By the corollary, G(x) = F(x) + C for some constant C. Therefore every antiderivative has the form F(x) + C.

sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.generalized-mean-value-theorem.rud.notes: Put h(t) = [f(b)-f(a)]g(t) - [g(b)-g(a)]f(t). Then h is continuous on [a,b], differentiable in (a,b), and h(a) = f(b)g(a) - f(a)g(b) = h(b). If h is constant, h'(x) = 0 for every x. Otherwise, h attains its maximum or minimum at some interior point x (by Theorem 4.16, EVT on compact sets), and Theorem 5.8 gives h'(x) = 0.

proof.geometric-series.stewart.notes: The partial sum is sₙ = a(1-rⁿ)/(1-r) for r ≠ 1. When |r| < 1, rⁿ → 0, so sₙ → a/(1-r). When |r| ≥ 1, the partial sums do not converge.

sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.heine-borel.rudin.notes: (a)→(b): E ⊂ k-cell I (bounded), I compact (2.40), E closed ⊂ I compact (2.35). (b)→(c): Theorem 2.37. (c)→(a): unbounded or not closed contradicts (c).

proof.horizontal-line-test.stewart.notes: Analogous to the vertical line test. If a horizontal line y = b intersects the graph at two points (x₁, b) and (x₂, b) with x₁ ≠ x₂, then f(x₁) = f(x₂) = b, contradicting injectivity.

sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.increasing-decreasing-test.rudin.notes: For any x1, x2 in (a,b) with x1 < x2, MVT gives f(x2) - f(x1) = (x2 - x1)f'(x) for some x between x1 and x2. If f'(x) >= 0, then f(x2) >= f(x1) (monotonically increasing). If f'(x) <= 0, then f(x2) <= f(x1) (monotonically decreasing).

proof.increasing-decreasing-test.stewart.notes: For x1 < x2 in the interval, MVT gives f(x2) - f(x1) = f'(c)(x2-x1) for some c in (x1,x2). If f'(c) > 0 then f(x2) > f(x1), so f is increasing. Analogous for decreasing.

sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.indefinite-integral-differentiabil.notes: Continuity: |F(y) - F(x)| = |integral_x^y f| <= M(y-x) by 6.12(c)(d). Differentiability at x_0: if f continuous at x_0, choose delta so |f(t) - f(x_0)| < epsilon for |t - x_0| < delta. Then |(F(t) - F(s))/(t-s) - f(x_0)| = |1/(t-s) integral_s^t [f(u) - f(x_0)] du| < epsilon.

proof.infinite-subset-compact-limit-poin.notes: If no point of K is a limit point of E, each q ∈ K has Vq with at most one point of E. No finite subcollection covers E ⊂ K — contradicts compactness.

proof.infinite-subset-countable.rudin.notes: Arrange A in sequence {xₙ}. Pick elements of E in order of their indices.

proof.integrability-criterion-consequenc.notes: (a) follows from Theorem 6.4. (b) uses |f(s_i) - f(t_i)| <= M_i - m_i. (c) uses L(P) <= sum f(t_i) Delta alpha_i <= U(P) and L(P) <= integral <= U(P).

proof.integrability-of-continuous-functi.notes: Stated without proof. Requires uniform continuity on a closed interval, which in turn requires the completeness of the reals.

sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

proof.integral-comparison.stewart.notes: If f(x) ≥ 0 then f(x_i*) ≥ 0 for all sample points, so each term f(x_i*)Δx ≥ 0, and the Riemann sum is ≥ 0. The limit preserves the inequality.

proof.integral-properties.stewart.notes: Each property follows from the corresponding limit law applied to the Riemann sum. For example, ∑[f(x_i*)+g(x_i*)]Δx = ∑f(x_i*)Δx + ∑g(x_i*)Δx, then take limits.

proof.integral-test.stewart.notes: By comparing the partial sums with upper and lower Riemann sums for the integral. Since f is decreasing, f(n+1) ≤ ∫_n^{n+1} f(x)dx ≤ f(n). Summing gives the comparison between partial sums and the integral. Bounded monotone sequences converge.

proof.integral-triangle-inequality-vecto.notes: |f| = (f_1^2 + ... + f_k^2)^{1/2} in R(alpha) by Theorem 6.11 applied twice (squaring, then square root). For the inequality, put y = integral f d alpha, compute |y|^2 = sum y_j integral f_j d alpha = integral (sum y_j f_j) d alpha <= |y| integral |f| d alpha by Schwarz inequality and Theorem 6.12(b). Divide by |y|.

proof.integrals-symmetric-functions.stew.notes: Split ∫_{-a}^a = ∫_{-a}^0 + ∫_0^a. In the first integral, substitute u = -x: ∫_{-a}^0 f(x)dx = ∫_a^0 f(-u)(-du) = ∫_0^a f(-u)du. If f is even, this equals ∫_0^a f(u)du, giving 2∫_0^a. If f is odd, this equals -∫_0^a f(u)du, giving 0.

proof.integrating-factor-method.stewart.notes: Let I(x) = e^{∫P(x)dx}. Then I'(x) = P(x)I(x) by the chain rule. Multiplying dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x) by I(x): I(x)dy/dx + I(x)P(x)y = I(x)Q(x). The left side is d/dx[I(x)y] by the product rule. Integrating both sides using FTC gives I(x)y = ∫I(x)Q(x)dx, so y = (1/I(x))∫I(x)Q(x)dx.

proof.integration-by-parts-definite.stew.notes: Apply the indefinite integration by parts formula and evaluate using FTC Part 2.

proof.integration-by-parts-riemann.rudin.notes: Put H(x) = F(x)G(x). Then H' = F'G + FG' = fG + Fg. Since f, g in R and F, G continuous (hence bounded), fG and Fg are in R by Theorem 6.13. Apply Theorem 6.21 to H.

proof.integration-by-parts.stewart.notes: By the product rule, d/dx[f(x)g(x)] = f(x)g'(x) + g(x)f'(x). Rearranging: f(x)g'(x) = d/dx[f(x)g(x)] - g(x)f'(x). Integrating both sides gives the integration by parts formula.

proof.integration-step-function.rudin.notes: Consider partition P = {a, s, x_2, b} with s < x_2. Then U(P,f,alpha) = M_2 and L(P,f,alpha) = m_2. As x_2 -> s, both converge to f(s) by continuity at s.

proof.integration-step-series.rudin.notes: Split alpha = alpha_1 + alpha_2 where alpha_1 is the first N terms and alpha_2 is the tail. By Theorems 6.12 and 6.15, integral f d alpha_1 = sum_{n=1}^N c_n f(s_n). Since alpha_2(b) - alpha_2(a) < epsilon, integral f d alpha_2 is small. Letting N -> infinity gives the result.

proof.intermediate-value-theorem.rudin.notes: By Theorem 2.47, [a,b] is connected. By Theorem 4.22, f([a,b]) is a connected subset of R¹. By Theorem 2.47 again, f([a,b]) contains every value between f(a) and f(b).

proof.intermediate-value-theorem.stewart.notes: Stewart states the IVT without proof in section 2.5, noting that a proof based on the Completeness Axiom of the real numbers is given in Appendix F. The proof relies on the least upper bound property, which is not developed in the main text.

proof.interval-uncountable.rudin.notes: [a,b] is a nonempty perfect set. Apply Theorem 2.43.

proof.inverse-graph-reflection.stewart.notes: Stewart argues that (a, b) is on the graph of f iff f(a) = b iff f⁻¹(b) = a iff (b, a) is on the graph of f⁻¹. The transformation (a, b) → (b, a) is precisely reflection about the line y = x.

proof.irrationality-of-sqrt-2.rudin.notes: Proof by contradiction: if p = m/n with m, n not both even, then p² = 2 implies m² = 2n², so m is even, hence m² divisible by 4, hence n² even, hence n even — contradiction. The gap in Q is shown by constructing q = (2p+2)/(p+2).

proof.k-cell-compact.rudin.notes: Bisect k-cell repeatedly. Get nested k-cells {Iₙ} with no finite subcover and diameter → 0. Their intersection point x* lies in some Gα, giving Iₙ ⊂ Gα for large n — contradiction.

proof.laws-of-exponents.stewart.notes: Stewart states the laws of exponents without proof in section 1.4, treating them as known results from precalculus extended to real exponents. A rigorous proof requires the construction of the real exponential via limits or the natural logarithm, which appears later in the text.

proof.laws-of-logarithms.stewart.notes: Stewart derives each law by applying the corresponding law of exponents through the inverse relationship between logarithm and exponential. For example, if logₐx = u and logₐy = v, then aᵘ = x and aᵛ = y, so xy = aᵘaᵛ = aᵘ⁺ᵛ, hence logₐ(xy) = u + v = logₐx + logₐy.

proof.lhopitals-rule.rudin.notes: Case -∞ < A < +∞: Choose r with A < r < q. By hypothesis (13), f'(x)/g'(x) < r near a. By the generalized MVT (5.9), (f(x)-f(y))/(g(x)-g(y)) = f'(t)/g'(t) < r for some t between x and y. For the 0/0 case: let x → a to get f(y)/g(y) <= r < q. For the ∞/∞ case: multiply by (g(x)-g(y))/g(x) and let x → a to get f(x)/g(x) < q. A symmetric argument with p < A gives the lower bound. Cases A = +∞ and A = -∞ are handled similarly.

proof.lhopitals-rule.stewart.notes: Stewart proves the 0/0 case for x→a using a generalized Mean Value Theorem (Cauchy MVT). For f(a) = g(a) = 0, there exists c between a and x with f(x)/g(x) = f'(c)/g'(c). As x→a, c→a, giving the result. The ∞/∞ case requires a more delicate argument not fully given in the text.

proof.limit-arithmetic-extended-real.rud.notes: Proof analogous to Theorem 4.4, using neighborhoods of ±∞. Rudin states it for completeness without giving a new proof.

proof.limit-arithmetic-functions-metric..notes: By Theorem 4.2, reduces to the analogous properties of sequences (Theorem 3.3: arithmetic of convergent sequences).

proof.limit-comparison-test.stewart.notes: Since aₙ/bₙ → c > 0, for large n we have (c/2)bₙ ≤ aₙ ≤ 2c·bₙ. The result follows from the Comparison Test applied in both directions.

proof.limit-cosx-minus-1-over-x.stewart.notes: Multiply numerator and denominator by (cos x + 1), use the identity cos²x - 1 = -sin²x, then apply the limit laws and the result lim sin(x)/x = 1.

proof.limit-exists-iff-one-sided-limits..notes: Follows from the epsilon-delta definitions: if both one-sided limits equal L, then for any epsilon the appropriate delta works for x on either side of a.

proof.limit-laws.stewart.notes: Stewart proves the sum law (law 1) in detail using the epsilon-delta definition in Appendix F. The other laws are proved similarly. The product law requires the triangle inequality and boundedness of one factor near the limit point.

proof.limit-one-over-x-at-infinity.stewa.notes: For any epsilon > 0, take N = (1/epsilon)^(1/r). Then x > N implies 1/x^r < epsilon.

proof.limit-point-infinite-points.rudin.notes: If N contains only finitely many points q₁,...,qₙ of E distinct from p, take r = min d(p,qₘ) > 0. Then Nr(p) contains no point of E except possibly p.

proof.limit-power-law.stewart.notes: Follows by repeated application of the product law (law 4) with g = f, using induction on n.

proof.limit-root-law.stewart.notes: Stewart states this law without a full proof in section 2.3. A rigorous proof requires continuity of the nth root function, which depends on the completeness of the real numbers.

proof.limit-sinx-over-x.stewart.notes: Stewart uses a geometric argument comparing areas in the unit circle: area of triangle <= area of sector <= area of outer triangle, yielding cos(x) <= sin(x)/x <= 1 for 0 < x < pi/2. The squeeze theorem then gives the result.

proof.local-extremum-at-critical.stewart.notes: If f has a local extremum at c, then either f'(c) does not exist (so c is critical by definition) or f'(c) exists and equals 0 by Fermat's theorem (so c is also critical).

proof.lower-leq-upper-integral.rudin.notes: Takes common refinement P* of arbitrary P_1, P_2. Then L(P_1) <= L(P*) <= U(P*) <= U(P_2). Taking sup over P_1 and inf over P_2 gives the result.

proof.lub-implies-glb.rudin.notes: Let L = set of lower bounds of B. Every x ∈ B is an upper bound of L, so L is bounded above. By LUB property, α = sup L exists. Show α ∈ L (α is a lower bound of B) and no β > α is in L.

proof.mean-value-inequality-vector.rudin.notes: Put z = f(b) - f(a) and define phi(t) = z . f(t) (inner product). Then phi is real-valued and continuous on [a,b], differentiable in (a,b). By the real MVT: phi(b) - phi(a) = (b - a)phi'(x) = (b - a)z . f'(x) for some x in (a,b). But phi(b) - phi(a) = z . z = |z|^2. By the Schwarz inequality: |z|^2 = (b - a)|z . f'(x)| <= (b - a)|z||f'(x)|. Hence |z| <= (b - a)|f'(x)|. Proof due to V. P. Havin.

proof.mean-value-theorem-integrals.stewa.notes: Since f is continuous on [a, b], by the Extreme Value Theorem it attains its absolute minimum m and maximum M. By the integral comparison property, m(b-a) ≤ ∫_a^b f(x) dx ≤ M(b-a), so m ≤ (1/(b-a))∫_a^b f(x) dx ≤ M. Since f is continuous and f_avg lies between m and M, the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees a number c in [a, b] with f(c) = f_avg.

sources.author: James Stewart

proof.mean-value-theorem.rudin.notes: Take g(x) = x in Theorem 5.9 (generalized MVT). Then [f(b) - f(a)] · 1 = [b - a] · f'(x) for some x in (a,b).

proof.mean-value-theorem.stewart.notes: Define h(x) = f(x) - [f(a) + ((f(b)-f(a))/(b-a))(x - a)]. Then h is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and h(a) = h(b) = 0. By Rolle's theorem, there exists c in (a,b) with h'(c) = 0, which gives f'(c) = (f(b)-f(a))/(b-a).

proof.mertens.rudin.notes: Write C_n = A_n B + γ_n where γ_n = a_0β_n + a_1β_{n-1} + ... + a_nβ_0. Show γ_n→0 using absolute convergence of Σa_n and β_n→0.

proof.monotone-convergence.rudin.notes: If increasing, let s = sup E (range). For every ε, s-ε < s_N ≤ s for some N; since increasing, s_n ∈ (s-ε, s] for all n>N. Converse from Thm 3.2(c).

proof.monotone-countable-discontinuities.notes: For f increasing, at each discontinuity x associate a rational r(x) with f(x−) < r(x) < f(x+). Since x₁ < x₂ implies f(x₁+) ≤ f(x₂−), we get r(x₁) ≠ r(x₂). This is a 1-1 map from discontinuities into Q, hence the set is at most countable.

proof.monotone-no-second-kind-discontinu.notes: Direct consequence of Theorem 4.29: both f(x+) and f(x−) exist at every point, so any discontinuity must be of the first kind.

proof.monotone-one-sided-limits.rudin.notes: Let A = sup{f(t): a<t<x}. Then A ≤ f(x). For any ε>0, ∃δ>0 with A−ε < f(x−δ) ≤ A. Monotonicity gives f(x−δ) ≤ f(t) ≤ A for x−δ<t<x, so |f(t)−A| < ε. Hence f(x−) = A. The inequality f(x+) ≤ f(y−) follows by comparing inf and sup over (x,y).

proof.monotonic-integrable-stieltjes.rud.notes: Since alpha is continuous, by IVT (Theorem 4.23) we can choose a partition with equal Delta alpha_i = [alpha(b) - alpha(a)]/n. If f is monotonically increasing, M_i = f(x_i), m_i = f(x_{i-1}), so U - L = [alpha(b) - alpha(a)]/n * [f(b) - f(a)] < epsilon for large n.

proof.monotonic-sequence-theorem.stewart.notes: Stewart states this theorem relies on the Completeness Axiom (every nonempty bounded above set of reals has a least upper bound). He does not provide a formal proof. The argument is: if {aₙ} is increasing and bounded above, let L = sup{aₙ}. Then for any ε > 0, L - ε is not an upper bound, so there exists N with aₙ > L - ε for n > N. Since aₙ ≤ L, we have |aₙ - L| < ε.

proof.multiplication-cancellation.rudin.notes: Analogous to the proof of Proposition 1.14 but using multiplicative axioms (M1)-(M5).

proof.n-tuples-countable.rudin.notes: Induction on n. Bₙ is union of countable sets of pairs (b,a) for b ∈ Bₙ₋₁.

proof.neighborhood-is-open.rudin.notes: For q ∈ Nr(p), set h = r - d(p,q). Then Nh(q) ⊂ Nr(p) by triangle inequality.

proof.nested-compact-nonempty.rudin.notes: Nested sequence satisfies finite intersection property trivially.

proof.nested-intervals.rudin.notes: Let E = {aₙ}, x = sup E. Then aₘ ≤ x ≤ bₘ for all m, so x ∈ every Iₘ.

proof.nested-k-cells.rudin.notes: Project each k-cell onto coordinate intervals. Apply Theorem 2.38 to each coordinate.

proof.net-change-theorem.stewart.notes: Direct application of FTC Part 2 with f = F'.

sources.author: James Stewart

proof.noncompact-counterexamples.rudin.notes: For bounded noncompact E: limit point x₀ ∉ E exists. (a) f(x) = 1/(x−x₀) is continuous, unbounded. (b) g(x) = 1/(1+(x−x₀)²) is bounded, sup=1 not attained. (c) f above is not uniformly continuous. For unbounded E: f(x)=x for (a), h(x)=x²/(1+x²) for (b).

proof.nonnegative-series-bounded.rudin.notes: Partial sums are monotonically increasing; bounded iff convergent by monotone convergence.

proof.nth-root-of-product.rudin.notes: Put α = a^{1/n}, β = b^{1/n}. Then ab = α^n β^n = (αβ)^n by commutativity. Uniqueness gives (ab)^{1/n} = αβ.

proof.open-iff-complement-closed.rudin.notes: If Eᶜ closed: x ∈ E means x not limit point of Eᶜ, so some neighborhood misses Eᶜ, i.e. lies in E. If E open: limit point of Eᶜ cannot be interior to E, so must be in Eᶜ.

proof.open-relative.rudin.notes: If E open relative to Y: for each p ∈ E take Vp = ball in X with d(p,q) < rp, set G = ⋃Vp. Then G open in X and E = G ∩ Y. Converse: if E = G ∩ Y with G open, each p ∈ E has neighborhood in G, intersect with Y gives E.

proof.ordered-field-properties.rudin.notes: Uses order-field compatibility axioms from Definition 1.17 and algebraic properties from Proposition 1.16.

proof.p-series-test.rudin.notes: If p≤0, terms don't → 0. If p>0, condensation gives Σ2^{(1-p)k} which is geometric with ratio 2^{1-p}.

proof.perfect-set-uncountable.rudin.notes: Assume P = {x₁,x₂,...}. Build nested closed balls Vₙ with Vₙ₊₁ ⊂ Vₙ, xₙ ∉ Vₙ₊₁, Vₙ ∩ P ≠ ∅. Then ⋂(Vₙ ∩ P) is nonempty but contains no xₙ — contradiction.

proof.power-rule-combined-chain.stewart.notes: Let y = u^n where u = g(x). By the chain rule, dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx) = nu^{n-1} · g'(x).

proof.power-rule.stewart.notes: For positive integer n, expand (x+h)^n using the Binomial Theorem: (x+h)^n = x^n + nx^{n-1}h + terms with h^2 or higher. Then f'(x) = lim(h→0) [(x+h)^n - x^n]/h = nx^{n-1}. The general case (all real n) is deferred to section 3.6 via logarithmic differentiation.

proof.power-series-boundary.rudin.notes: Put a_n = z^n, b_n = c_n. Partial sums of z^n bounded by 2/|1-z| when |z|=1, z≠1.

proof.power-series-convergence.stewart.notes: Stewart sketches the proof: if the series converges at x = d ≠ a, then cₙdⁿ is bounded, say |cₙdⁿ| ≤ M. For |x| < |d|, we have |cₙxⁿ| ≤ M|x/d|ⁿ, a convergent geometric series. The radius of convergence is then R = sup{|x-a| : series converges}. Full details of the supremum argument are omitted.

proof.power-series-differentiation-integ.notes: Stewart states this theorem without proof, noting it requires uniform convergence concepts from advanced analysis. The proof that term-by-term differentiation preserves convergence and yields the correct derivative requires the Weierstrass M-test and uniform convergence of the differentiated series.

proof.product-absolute-value-integrable..notes: (a) Take phi(t) = t^2 to get f^2 in R(alpha). Then use 4fg = (f+g)^2 - (f-g)^2 and linearity. (b) Take phi(t) = |t| to get |f| in R(alpha). For the inequality, choose c = +-1 so that c * integral f >= 0, then |integral f| = integral cf <= integral |f|.

proof.product-rule.rudin.notes: Let h = fg. Then h(t) - h(x) = f(t)[g(t) - g(x)] + g(x)[f(t) - f(x)]. Dividing by t - x and noting f(t) → f(x) as t → x (by Theorem 5.2), the product rule follows from Theorem 4.4 (limit laws).

proof.product-rule.stewart.notes: Add and subtract f(x+h)g(x): [f(x+h)g(x+h) - f(x)g(x)]/h = f(x+h)[g(x+h)-g(x)]/h + g(x)[f(x+h)-f(x)]/h. As h→0, f(x+h)→f(x) (by continuity, since f is differentiable), yielding f(x)g'(x) + g(x)f'(x).

proof.quotient-rule.rudin.notes: Let h = f/g. Then (h(t) - h(x))/(t - x) = (1/(g(t)g(x)))[g(x)(f(t)-f(x))/(t-x) - f(x)(g(t)-g(x))/(t-x)]. Letting t → x, applying Theorems 4.4 and 5.2, we obtain (c).

proof.quotient-rule.stewart.notes: [f(x+h)/g(x+h) - f(x)/g(x)]/h = [f(x+h)g(x) - f(x)g(x+h)] / [h · g(x+h)g(x)]. Add and subtract f(x)g(x) in the numerator, apply limit laws, and use continuity of g to get g(x+h)→g(x).

proof.ratio-test.rudin.notes: (a) |a_{n+1}|<β|a_n| gives |a_n| < |a_N|β^{n-N}, compare geometric. (b) |a_n| increasing so a_n ↛ 0.

proof.ratio-test.stewart.notes: Part (i): If L < 1, pick r with L < r < 1. For large n, |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| < r, so |aₙ| < |aₙ|rⁿ⁻ᴺ for n ≥ N. By comparison with a convergent geometric series, ∑ |aₙ| converges. Part (ii): For large n, |aₙ₊₁| > |aₙ|, so aₙ does not approach 0; the series diverges by the Divergence Test.

proof.rationals-countable.rudin.notes: Every rational r = b/a where (a,b) are integers. Apply Theorem 2.13 with n=2.

proof.refinement-upper-lower-sums.rudin.notes: Proves by induction on the number of extra points. Adding one point x* to [x_{i-1}, x_i] splits the infimum into two parts, each >= m_i, so L increases. Analogous for U.

proof.riemann-rearrangement.rudin.notes: Both ΣP_n and ΣQ_n diverge. Construct rearrangement by alternately adding positive terms until exceeding β_n, then negative terms until below α_n. Since P_n→0, Q_n→0, the partial sums oscillate to desired limits.

proof.riemann-stieltjes-integrability-cr.notes: Forward: U-L < epsilon implies upper and lower integrals differ by < epsilon, hence they are equal. Converse: if f in R(alpha), choose P_1, P_2 such that U(P_2) and L(P_1) are close to the integral, then common refinement works.

proof.riemann-stieltjes-integral-propert.notes: Part (a) linearity: uses L(P,f1) + L(P,f2) <= L(P,f) <= U(P,f) <= U(P,f1) + U(P,f2) and the integrability criterion. Parts (b)-(e) follow similarly. For part (c), restrict to partitions containing point c.

proof.rolles-theorem.stewart.notes: Case 1: f(x) = f(a) for all x in [a,b], then f is constant and f'(c) = 0 for any c. Case 2: f(x) > f(a) for some x, then by EVT f attains a maximum at some c in (a,b) (not an endpoint since f(a) = f(b)). By Fermat's theorem, f'(c) = 0. Case 3: analogous with minimum.

proof.root-test-stronger-than-ratio.rudi.notes: If c_{n+1}/c_n ≤ β for n≥N, then c_n ≤ c_N β^{n-N}, so n-th root ≤ (c_N β^{-N})^{1/n} · β → β.

proof.root-test.rudin.notes: α<1: choose β with α<β<1, then |a_n|<β^n eventually, compare with geometric. α>1: |a_n|>1 infinitely often, terms don't → 0.

proof.root-test.stewart.notes: Part (i): If L < 1, pick r with L < r < 1. For large n, ⁿ√|aₙ| < r, so |aₙ| < rⁿ. By comparison with the convergent geometric series ∑ rⁿ, the series ∑ |aₙ| converges.

proof.schwarz-inequality.rudin.notes: Put A = Σ|a_j|², B = Σ|b_j|², C = Σa_j b̄_j. If B = 0, trivial. Otherwise expand Σ|Ba_j - Cb_j|² = B²A - B|C|² = B(AB-|C|²) ≥ 0. Since B > 0, AB - |C|² ≥ 0.

proof.second-derivative-test.stewart.notes: If f'(c) = 0 and f''(c) > 0, then f is concave up near c. Since the tangent line at c is horizontal (slope 0) and the curve is above the tangent, c is a local minimum. Analogous for max.

proof.sequential-characterization-functi.notes: Forward: given ε-δ limit, any sequence p_n → p with p_n ≠ p eventually enters the δ-ball, so f(p_n) enters the ε-ball. Converse: contrapositive — if ε-δ fails, construct a sequence with δ_n = 1/n witnessing failure.

proof.series-addition.rudin.notes: A_n + B_n = Σ(a_k + b_k); limits add.

proof.special-sequence-limits.rudin.notes: (a) Archimedean. (b) Binomial theorem gives 0 < x_n ≤ (p-1)/n. (c) Binomial gives 0 ≤ x_n ≤ √(2/(n-1)). (d) Choose k>α, binomial lower bound on (1+p)^n. (e) α=0 in (d).

proof.squeeze-theorem.stewart.notes: Given epsilon > 0, since lim f(x) = L and lim h(x) = L, there exist delta_1 and delta_2 such that f(x) and h(x) are within epsilon of L. Taking delta = min(delta_1, delta_2), the inequality f(x) <= g(x) <= h(x) forces g(x) within epsilon of L.

proof.stieltjes-riemann-reduction.rudin.notes: Apply Theorem 6.6 to alpha' to get a partition P with U(P,alpha') - L(P,alpha') < epsilon. MVT gives t_i with Delta alpha_i = alpha'(t_i) Delta x_i. By Theorem 6.7(b), sum |alpha'(s_i) - alpha'(t_i)| Delta x_i < epsilon. Then |U(P,f,alpha) - U(P,f alpha')| <= M epsilon. Since this holds for all refinements, the upper integrals agree, and similarly for lower integrals.

proof.subsequence-compact.rudin.notes: (a) If range finite, constant subsequence; if infinite, limit point exists by Thm 2.37, pick n_i with d(p, p_{n_i}) < 1/i. (b) Bounded subset of R^k lies in compact set.

proof.subsequential-limits-closed.rudin.notes: Let q be limit point of E*. Construct subsequence converging to q by choosing n_i with d(q, p_{n_i}) ≤ 2^{1-i}δ.

proof.substitution-rule-definite.stewart.notes: Let F be an antiderivative of f. Then by FTC Part 2: ∫_a^b f(g(x))g'(x)dx = F(g(x))|_a^b = F(g(b)) - F(g(a)) = ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u)du.

proof.substitution-rule.stewart.notes: If F is an antiderivative of f, then by the chain rule d/dx[F(g(x))] = F'(g(x)) g'(x) = f(g(x)) g'(x). Therefore ∫ f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = F(g(x)) + C = F(u) + C = ∫ f(u) du.

proof.sum-rule.stewart.notes: d/dx[f(x)+g(x)] = lim(h→0) {[f(x+h)+g(x+h)] - [f(x)+g(x)]}/h = lim(h→0) [f(x+h)-f(x)]/h + lim(h→0) [g(x+h)-g(x)]/h = f'(x) + g'(x) by the sum law for limits.

proof.summation-by-parts.rudin.notes: Abel's summation formula: write a_n = A_n - A_{n-1}, substitute and rearrange.

proof.sup-in-closure.rudin.notes: If y ∉ E, for every h > 0 there exists x ∈ E with y-h < x < y (else y-h is upper bound). So y is limit point of E, hence y ∈ E̅.

proof.taylor-convergence.stewart.notes: Taylor's inequality |Rₙ(x)| ≤ M|x-a|ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)! is derived from the Lagrange form of the remainder (which uses the MVT applied to the remainder function). Since |x-a|ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)! → 0 for any fixed x (by the Squeeze Theorem, comparing with the convergent series for eˣ), we get Rₙ(x) → 0.

proof.taylor-theorem.rudin.notes: Let M be defined by f(beta) = P(beta) + M(beta - alpha)^n, and put g(t) = f(t) - P(t) - M(t - alpha)^n. Then g^(n)(t) = f^(n)(t) - n!M and g(alpha) = g'(alpha) = ... = g^(n-1)(alpha) = 0. Since g(beta) = 0, MVT gives g'(x1) = 0 for some x1 between alpha and beta. Since g'(alpha) = 0, MVT gives g''(x2) = 0 for some x2 between alpha and x1. After n steps: g^(n)(xn) = 0, so f^(n)(xn) = n!M.

proof.unions-intersections-open-closed.r.notes: (a) x ∈ ⋃Gα means x ∈ some Gα, interior there, hence interior in union. (b) By De Morgan + (a). (c) Take r = min(r₁,...,rₙ). (d) By De Morgan + (c).

proof.uniqueness-of-function-limit.rudin.notes: Follows from Theorem 3.2(b) (uniqueness of sequence limits) and the sequential characterization (Theorem 4.2).

proof.vertical-line-test.stewart.notes: Stewart argues directly from the definition of function: if a vertical line x = a intersects the curve at two points, then the curve assigns two values to a, contradicting the definition of function.

proof.zero-derivative-constant.stewart.notes: For any x1 < x2 in (a,b), MVT gives f(x2) - f(x1) = f'(c)(x2-x1) for some c in (x1,x2). Since f'(c) = 0, f(x2) = f(x1).

natural.en: The axioms for addition imply: (a) If x + y = x + z then y = z. (b) If x + y = x then y = 0. (c) If x + y = 0 then y = -x. (d) -(-x) = x.

proposition.addition-cancellation.notes: Rudin Proposition 1.14. (b) asserts uniqueness of additive identity, (c) asserts uniqueness of additive inverse.

natural.en: If f is a one-to-one function with inverse f⁻¹, then f⁻¹(f(x)) = x for every x in the domain of f, and f(f⁻¹(x)) = x for every x in the domain of f⁻¹.
natural.es: Si f es una función inyectiva con inversa f⁻¹, entonces f⁻¹(f(x)) = x para todo x en el dominio de f, y f(f⁻¹(x)) = x para todo x en el dominio de f⁻¹.

proposition.cancellation-equations.notes: Stewart presents the cancellation equations as direct consequences of the definition of inverse function in section 1.5.

For any positive number a ≠ 1, we have logₐx = ln(x)/ln(a) for all x > 0.
natural.es: Para cualquier número positivo a ≠ 1, se tiene logₐx = ln(x)/ln(a) para todo x > 0.

proposition.change-of-base-formula.notes: Stewart presents the change of base formula in section 1.5, noting it allows computing any logarithm using natural logarithms.

natural.en: Compact subsets of metric spaces are closed.

natural.en: (a) If f''(x) > 0 for all x in I, then the graph of f is concave upward on I. (b) If f''(x) < 0 for all x in I, then the graph of f is concave downward on I.
natural.es: (a) Si f''(x) > 0 para toda x en I, entonces la gráfica de f es cóncava hacia arriba en I. (b) Si f''(x) < 0 para toda x en I, entonces la gráfica de f es cóncava hacia abajo en I.

proposition.concavity-test.notes: f'' > 0 means f' is increasing, so the slope of the tangent line is increasing, hence the curve lies above its tangents.

p \text{ limit point of } E \;\Rightarrow\;
\bigl(f \text{ continuous at } p \iff \lim_{x \to p} f(x) = f(p)\bigr)

natural.en: In the situation of Definition 4.5, assume also that p is a limit point of E. Then f is continuous at p if and only if lim_{x→p} f(x) = f(p).

proposition.continuity-limit-point-equiv.notes: Reclassified from theorem to proposition: trivial comparison of Definitions 4.1 and 4.5, serving as a utility bridge fact.

title.en: Continuity Equals Limit at Limit Points

natural.en: (a) A sequence {x_n} in R^k converges to x if and only if each component sequence converges to the corresponding component of x. (b) The algebraic limit laws extend to R^k: limits of sums, scalar multiples, and inner products behave as expected.

proposition.convergent-sequence-properti.latex: p_n \to p \iff \forall \varepsilon > 0,\; \exists N : n \geq N \implies d(p_n, p) < \varepsilon

natural.en: (a) {p_n} converges to p if and only if every neighborhood of p contains all but finitely many terms of {p_n}. (b) If {p_n} converges, its limit is unique. (c) If {p_n} converges, then {p_n} is bounded. (d) If E is a subset of a metric space X and p is a limit point of E, then there is a sequence {p_n} in E such that p_n → p.
Let {Eα} be a collection of sets. Then (⋃α Eα)ᶜ = ⋂α Eαᶜ.

proposition.de-morgan.notes: Theorem 2.22 in Rudin. De Morgan's law for arbitrary collections of sets.

natural.en: (a) The diameter of the closure of E equals the diameter of E. (b) If {K_n} is a sequence of compact sets in a metric space X with K_n ⊃ K_{n+1} and diam K_n → 0, then the intersection of all K_n consists of exactly one point.
If f is a polynomial or rational function and a is in the domain of f, then lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).
natural.es: Si f es una función polinomial o racional y a está en el dominio de f, entonces lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a).

proposition.direct-substitution-property.notes: Stewart derives this from the limit laws. It is the basis for direct evaluation of limits for polynomial and rational functions.

natural.en: The field axioms imply, for any x, y, z ∈ F: (a) 0x = 0. (b) If x ≠ 0 and y ≠ 0 then xy ≠ 0. (c) (-x)y = -(xy) = x(-y). (d) (-x)(-y) = xy.

proposition.field-zero-product.notes: Rudin Proposition 1.16. These are basic consequences of the field axioms that hold in any field.

title.en: Field Properties of Zero and Negation

natural.en: Suppose that c is a critical number of a continuous function f. (a) If f' changes from positive to negative at c, then f has a local maximum at c. (b) If f' changes from negative to positive at c, then f has a local minimum at c. (c) If f' does not change sign at c, then f has no local extremum at c.
natural.es: Suponga que c es un número crítico de una función continua f. (a) Si f' cambia de positiva a negativa en c, entonces f tiene un máximo local en c. (b) Si f' cambia de negativa a positiva en c, entonces f tiene un mínimo local en c. (c) Si f' no cambia de signo en c, entonces f no tiene extremo local en c.

proposition.first-derivative-test.notes: Follows from the increasing/decreasing test applied to intervals on either side of the critical number.

natural.en: A function is one-to-one if and only if no horizontal line intersects its graph more than once.
natural.es: Una función es inyectiva si y sólo si ninguna línea horizontal corta su gráfica más de una vez.

proposition.horizontal-line-test.notes: Reclassified from definition to proposition. The horizontal line test is a criterion for injectivity, not the introduction of a new mathematical object.

natural.en: (a) If f'(x) > 0 on an interval, then f is increasing on that interval. (b) If f'(x) < 0 on an interval, then f is decreasing on that interval.
natural.es: (a) Si f'(x) > 0 en un intervalo, entonces f es creciente en ese intervalo. (b) Si f'(x) < 0 en un intervalo, entonces f es decreciente en ese intervalo.

proposition.increasing-decreasing-test.notes: Direct consequence of the Mean Value Theorem. Rudin (5.11) states three parts: (a) f' >= 0 implies monotonically increasing, (b) f' = 0 implies constant, (c) f' <= 0 implies monotonically decreasing. Stewart uses strict inequalities (f' > 0 implies increasing, f' < 0 implies decreasing). Rudin's non-strict version subsumes Stewart's strict version.

natural.en: Every infinite subset of a countable set A is countable.

natural.en: (a) If U(P,f,alpha) - L(P,f,alpha) < epsilon holds for some P and epsilon, then it holds for every refinement of P. (b) If this holds for P = {x_0,...,x_n} and s_i, t_i are arbitrary points in [x_{i-1}, x_i], then sum |f(s_i) - f(t_i)| Delta alpha_i < epsilon. (c) If f in R(alpha) and the hypotheses of (b) hold, then |sum f(t_i) Delta alpha_i - integral f d alpha| < epsilon.

If f and g are integrable on [a, b]: 1. If f(x) ≥ 0 for a ≤ x ≤ b, then ∫_a^b f(x) dx ≥ 0. 2. If f(x) ≥ g(x) for a ≤ x ≤ b, then ∫_a^b f(x) dx ≥ ∫_a^b g(x) dx. 3. If m ≤ f(x) ≤ M for a ≤ x ≤ b, then m(b-a) ≤ ∫_a^b f(x) dx ≤ M(b-a).
natural.es: Si f y g son integrables en [a, b]: 1. Si f(x) ≥ 0 para a ≤ x ≤ b, entonces ∫_a^b f(x) dx ≥ 0. 2. Si f(x) ≥ g(x) para a ≤ x ≤ b, entonces ∫_a^b f(x) dx ≥ ∫_a^b g(x) dx. 3. Si m ≤ f(x) ≤ M para a ≤ x ≤ b, entonces m(b-a) ≤ ∫_a^b f(x) dx ≤ M(b-a).

proposition.integral-comparison.notes: Follow from the definition: non-negative integrands produce non-negative Riemann sums, and limits preserve inequalities.

natural.en: Let f and g be integrable functions and c a constant. Then: 1. ∫_a^b c dx = c(b - a). 2. ∫_a^b [f(x) + g(x)] dx = ∫_a^b f(x) dx + ∫_a^b g(x) dx. 3. ∫_a^b cf(x) dx = c ∫_a^b f(x) dx. 4. ∫_a^b [f(x) - g(x)] dx = ∫_a^b f(x) dx - ∫_a^b g(x) dx. 5. ∫_a^c f(x) dx + ∫_c^b f(x) dx = ∫_a^b f(x) dx.
natural.es: Sean f y g funciones integrables y c una constante. Entonces: 1. ∫_a^b c dx = c(b - a). 2. ∫_a^b [f(x) + g(x)] dx = ∫_a^b f(x) dx + ∫_a^b g(x) dx. 3. ∫_a^b cf(x) dx = c ∫_a^b f(x) dx. 4. ∫_a^b [f(x) - g(x)] dx = ∫_a^b f(x) dx - ∫_a^b g(x) dx. 5. ∫_a^c f(x) dx + ∫_c^b f(x) dx = ∫_a^b f(x) dx.

proposition.integral-properties.notes: These properties follow from the linearity of limits and the definition of the definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums.

natural.en: If f has a local extremum at c, then c is a critical number of f.
natural.es: Si f tiene un extremo local en c, entonces c es un número crítico de f.

natural.en: Let A be a countable set, and let Bₙ be the set of all n-tuples (a₁,...,aₙ) where aₖ ∈ A. Then Bₙ is countable.

natural.en: In every ordered field: (a) If x > 0 then -x < 0, and vice versa. (b) If x > 0 and y < z then xy < xz. (c) If x < 0 and y < z then xy > xz. (d) If x ≠ 0 then x² > 0; in particular 1 > 0. (e) If 0 < x < y then 0 < 1/y < 1/x.

proposition.ordered-field-properties.notes: Rudin Proposition 1.18. Standard ordering properties that hold in any ordered field.

natural.es: Suponga que f'' es continua cerca de c. (a) Si f'(c) = 0 y f''(c) > 0, entonces f tiene un mínimo local en c. (b) Si f'(c) = 0 y f''(c) < 0, entonces f tiene un máximo local en c.

proposition.second-derivative-test.notes: When f''(c) > 0, f is concave up near c, so the tangent line at c lies below the graph, meaning c is a local minimum.

natural.en: A curve in the xy-plane is the graph of a function of x if and only if no vertical line intersects the curve more than once.
natural.es: Una curva en el plano xy es la gráfica de una función de x si y sólo si ninguna línea vertical corta a la curva en más de un punto.

proposition.vertical-line-test.notes: Reclassified from definition to proposition. The vertical line test is a criterion for determining whether a curve represents a function, not the introduction of a new mathematical object.

natural.es: Si la serie alternante ∑_{n=1}^∞ (-1)ⁿ⁻¹ bₙ (con bₙ > 0) satisface (i) bₙ₊₁ ≤ bₙ para todo n y (ii) lim(n→∞) bₙ = 0, entonces la serie converge.

sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: If gamma' is continuous on [a, b], then gamma is rectifiable and Lambda(gamma) = integral_a^b |gamma'(t)| dt.

title.en: Arc Length Formula for Continuously Differentiable Curves

theorem.archimedean-density.latex:
(a)\; \forall x>0,\; \forall y \in \mathbb{R},\; \exists n \in \mathbb{Z}^+:\; nx > y
\qquad
(b)\; x < y \implies \exists p \in \mathbb{Q}:\; x < p < y

natural.en: (a) If x ∈ R, y ∈ R, and x > 0, then there is a positive integer n such that nx > y (archimedean property). (b) If x ∈ R, y ∈ R, and x < y, then there exists a p ∈ Q such that x < p < y (density of Q in R).

theorem.archimedean-density.notes: Rudin Theorem 1.20. Both parts are derived from the least-upper-bound property.

title.en: Archimedean Property and Density of Q in R

natural.en: Let A be the set of all sequences whose elements are the digits 0 and 1. Then A is uncountable.

theorem.binary-sequences-uncountable.notes: Theorem 2.14 in Rudin. Cantor's diagonal argument.

title.en: The Set of All Binary Sequences is Uncountable

natural.en: Every bounded infinite subset of Rk has a limit point in Rk.

theorem.bolzano-weierstrass.notes: Theorem 2.42 in Rudin. Immediate consequence of the Heine-Borel theorem.

theorem.cauchy-condensation-test.latex: a_1 \geq a_2 \geq \cdots \geq 0 \implies \left( \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \text{ conv.} \iff \sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^k a_{2^k} \text{ conv.} \right)

natural.en: If a_1 ≥ a_2 ≥ ... ≥ 0, then Σa_n converges if and only if Σ2^k a_{2^k} converges.

(a) In any metric space, every convergent sequence is a Cauchy sequence. (b) If X is a compact metric space, then every Cauchy sequence in X converges. (c) In R^k, a sequence converges if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence.

If g is differentiable at x and f is differentiable at g(x), then the composite function F = f ∘ g defined by F(x) = f(g(x)) is differentiable at x and F' is given by F'(x) = f'(g(x)) · g'(x). In Leibniz notation, if y = f(u) and u = g(x) are differentiable functions, then dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx).
natural.es: Si g es diferenciable en x y f es diferenciable en g(x), entonces la función compuesta F = f ∘ g definida por F(x) = f(g(x)) es diferenciable en x y F' se obtiene mediante F'(x) = f'(g(x)) · g'(x). En notación de Leibniz, si y = f(u) y u = g(x) son funciones diferenciables, entonces dy/dx = (dy/du)(du/dx).

theorem.chain-rule.notes: One of the most important rules in calculus. Stewart proves it using an increment formulation that avoids dividing by Δu = 0. Rudin (5.5) uses the same approach with error functions u(t), v(s) and the continuity of f to conclude s → y as t → x.
