sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: Suppose phi is a strictly increasing continuous function that maps [A, B] onto [a, b]. Suppose alpha is monotonically increasing on [a, b] and f in R(alpha) on [a, b]. Define beta(y) = alpha(phi(y)) and g(y) = f(phi(y)). Then g in R(beta) and integral_A^B g d beta = integral_a^b f d alpha.

theorem.change-of-variable-integral.notes: Special case: taking alpha(x) = x gives beta = phi, and if phi' in R on [A,B], Theorem 6.17 yields the classical substitution formula integral_a^b f(x) dx = integral_A^B f(phi(y)) phi'(y) dy.

title.en: Change of Variable for Riemann-Stieltjes Integrals

theorem.characterization-lim-sup.latex: s^* \in E \text{ and } x > s^* \implies \exists N : n \geq N \implies s_n < x

natural.en: Let {s_n} be a real sequence, and let E* be the set of all subsequential limits (including ±∞). Let s* = sup E* = lim sup s_n. Then: (a) s* ∈ E*; (b) if x > s*, there exists N such that n ≥ N implies s_n < x. Moreover, s* is the only number with both properties (a) and (b).

theorem.compact-uniform-continuity.latex:
f : X \to Y \text{ continuous},\; X \text{ compact}
\;\Rightarrow\; f \text{ uniformly continuous on } X

natural.en: Let f be a continuous mapping of a compact metric space X into a metric space Y. Then f is uniformly continuous on X.

theorem.compact-uniform-continuity.notes: The proof uses the Lebesgue covering lemma idea: extract a finite subcover from neighborhoods, then take δ as half the minimum radius.

title.en: Continuous on Compact Implies Uniformly Continuous

natural.en: Suppose K ⊂ Y ⊂ X. Then K is compact relative to X if and only if K is compact relative to Y.

theorem.compactness-relative.notes: Theorem 2.33 in Rudin. Compactness is an intrinsic property, not dependent on the ambient space.

title.en: Compactness is Independent of the Ambient Space

natural.en: Suppose ∑ aₙ and ∑ bₙ are series with positive terms. (i) If ∑ bₙ converges and aₙ ≤ bₙ for all n, then ∑ aₙ also converges. (ii) If ∑ bₙ diverges and aₙ ≥ bₙ for all n, then ∑ aₙ also diverges.
natural.es: Suponga que ∑ aₙ y ∑ bₙ son series con términos positivos. (i) Si ∑ bₙ converge y aₙ ≤ bₙ para todo n, entonces ∑ aₙ también converge. (ii) Si ∑ bₙ diverge y aₙ ≥ bₙ para todo n, entonces ∑ aₙ también diverge.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: Suppose f and g are continuous functions with f(x) ≥ g(x) ≥ 0 for x ≥ a. (a) If ∫_a^∞ f(x) dx is convergent, then ∫_a^∞ g(x) dx is also convergent. (b) If ∫_a^∞ g(x) dx is divergent, then ∫_a^∞ f(x) dx is also divergent.
natural.es: Suponga que f y g son funciones continuas con f(x) ≥ g(x) ≥ 0 para x ≥ a. (a) Si ∫_a^∞ f(x) dx es convergente, entonces ∫_a^∞ g(x) dx también es convergente. (b) Si ∫_a^∞ g(x) dx es divergente, entonces ∫_a^∞ f(x) dx también es divergente.

theorem.comparison-theorem-integrals.notes: The comparison theorem is analogous to the comparison test for series (Chapter 11). Stewart states it without detailed proof, relying on the monotone convergence property of bounded increasing sequences.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.es: Teorema de comparación para integrales impropias

natural.en: Let z and w be complex numbers. Then (a) |z| > 0 unless z = 0, |0| = 0, (b) |z̄| = |z|, (c) |zw| = |z||w|, (d) |Re z| ≤ |z|, (e) |z + w| ≤ |z| + |w| (triangle inequality).

theorem.complex-absolute-value-propertie.notes: Rudin Theorem 1.33. Part (e) is the triangle inequality for C.

natural.en: If a and b are real, then (a, b) = a + bi.

theorem.complex-algebraic-form.notes: Rudin Theorem 1.29. Bridges ordered-pair definition with classical notation.

natural.en: The definitions of addition and multiplication of complex numbers (ordered pairs of reals) turn the set of all complex numbers into a field, with (0, 0) and (1, 0) in the role of 0 and 1.

theorem.complex-field.notes: Rudin Theorem 1.25. Proof verifies all field axioms directly.

natural.en: Suppose f is in R(alpha) on [a, b], m <= f <= M, phi is continuous on [m, M], and h(x) = phi(f(x)) on [a, b]. Then h is in R(alpha) on [a, b].

title.en: Composition with Continuous Function Preserves Integrability

natural.en: If z and w are complex, then (a) conjugate of (z + w) equals conjugate(z) + conjugate(w), (b) conjugate of (zw) equals conjugate(z) · conjugate(w), (c) z + conjugate(z) = 2 Re(z) and z - conjugate(z) = 2i Im(z), (d) z · conjugate(z) is real and positive (except when z = 0).

theorem.conjugate-properties.notes: Rudin Theorem 1.31. Part (d) is crucial for defining |z|.

natural.en: A subset E of the real line R¹ is connected if and only if: whenever x ∈ E, y ∈ E, and x < z < y, then z ∈ E.

theorem.connected-subsets-of-r.notes: Theorem 2.47 in Rudin. Connected subsets of R are precisely the intervals.

title.en: Characterization of Connected Subsets of R

natural.en: If c is a constant and f is a differentiable function, then d/dx[cf(x)] = c d/dx f(x).
natural.es: Si c es una constante y f es una función diferenciable, entonces d/dx[cf(x)] = c d/dx f(x).

theorem.constant-multiple-rule.notes: Proved using the definition of the derivative and the constant multiple law for limits.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: Let f and g be complex continuous functions on a metric space X. Then f + g, fg, and f/g are continuous on X. In the last case, g(x) ≠ 0 for all x ∈ X.

(a) Let f₁, ..., f_k be real functions on a metric space X, and let f be the mapping into R^k defined by f(x) = (f₁(x), ..., f_k(x)). Then f is continuous if and only if each f_j is continuous. (b) If f and g are continuous mappings of X into R^k, then f + g and f · g are continuous on X.

title.en: Continuity of Vector-Valued Functions via Components

natural.en: If f and g are continuous at a and c is a constant, then the following functions are also continuous at a: f + g, f - g, cf, fg, and f/g (if g(a) ≠ 0).
natural.es: Si f y g son continuas en a y c es una constante, entonces las siguientes funciones también son continuas en a: f + g, f - g, cf, fg, y f/g (si g(a) ≠ 0).

theorem.continuity-of-combinations.notes: Follows directly from the limit laws applied to the definition of continuity.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: If f is continuous at b and lim(x→a) g(x) = b, then lim(x→a) f(g(x)) = f(b). In other words, lim(x→a) f(g(x)) = f(lim(x→a) g(x)). In particular, if g is continuous at a and f is continuous at g(a), then the composite function f ∘ g is continuous at a.
natural.es: Si f es continua en b y lim(x→a) g(x) = b, entonces lim(x→a) f(g(x)) = f(b). En otras palabras, lim(x→a) f(g(x)) = f(lim(x→a) g(x)). En particular, si g es continua en a y f es continua en g(a), entonces la función compuesta f ∘ g es continua en a.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

theorem.continuity-of-composition-metric.latex:
f \text{ continuous at } p,\; g \text{ continuous at } f(p)
\;\Rightarrow\; g \circ f \text{ continuous at } p

natural.en: Suppose X, Y, Z are metric spaces, E ⊂ X, f maps E into Y, g maps f(E) into Z, and h(x) = g(f(x)) for x ∈ E. If f is continuous at p ∈ E and g is continuous at f(p), then h is continuous at p.

theorem.continuity-of-composition-metric.notes: Strictly more general than Stewart's theorem.continuity-of-composition which is stated for real functions. The proof structure is the same (chain two ε-δ arguments).

theorem.continuity-open-preimage.latex:
f : X \to Y \text{ continuous} \;\iff\;
V \text{ open in } Y \Rightarrow f^{-1}(V) \text{ open in } X

natural.en: A mapping f of a metric space X into a metric space Y is continuous on X if and only if f⁻¹(V) is open in X for every open set V in Y.

theorem.continuity-open-preimage.notes: This topological characterization of continuity is fundamental. It motivates the general definition of continuity in topology.

theorem.continuous-bijection-compact-inv.latex:
f : X \xrightarrow{\text{cont., 1-1, onto}} Y,\; X \text{ compact}
\;\Rightarrow\; f^{-1} : Y \to X \text{ continuous}

natural.en: Suppose f is a continuous 1-1 mapping of a compact metric space X onto a metric space Y. Then the inverse mapping f⁻¹ (defined by f⁻¹(f(x)) = x for x ∈ X) is a continuous mapping of Y onto X.

title.en: Continuous Bijection from Compact Space has Continuous Inverse

natural.en: If f is a continuous mapping of a compact metric space X into R^k, then f(X) is closed and bounded. Thus f is bounded.

title.en: Continuous Image of Compact Set into R^k is Closed and Bounded

theorem.continuous-image-compact.latex:
f : X \to Y \text{ continuous},\; X \text{ compact}
\;\Rightarrow\; f(X) \text{ compact}

natural.en: Suppose f is a continuous mapping of a compact metric space X into a metric space Y. Then f(X) is compact.

theorem.continuous-image-compact.notes: Fundamental result connecting continuity and compactness. Many important theorems (4.15, 4.16, 4.17, 4.19) follow as consequences.

title.en: Continuous Image of a Compact Set is Compact

theorem.continuous-image-connected.latex:
f : X \to Y \text{ continuous},\; E \subset X \text{ connected}
\;\Rightarrow\; f(E) \text{ connected}

natural.en: If f is a continuous mapping of a metric space X into a metric space Y, and if E is a connected subset of X, then f(E) is connected.

theorem.continuous-image-connected.notes: Fundamental result connecting continuity and connectedness. The Intermediate Value Theorem follows as a corollary via the characterization of connected subsets of R (Theorem 2.47).

title.en: Continuous Image of a Connected Set is Connected

natural.en: If f is continuous on [a, b] then f is in R(alpha) on [a, b] for every monotonically increasing alpha.

theorem.continuous-integrable-stieltjes.notes: This is strictly more general than the Stewart version (theorem.integrability-of-continuous-functions) which only treats the Riemann integral (alpha(x) = x). The proof uses uniform continuity on [a, b] (compact, hence Theorem 4.19 applies).

natural.en: Let {Eₙ} be a sequence of countable sets and S = ⋃Eₙ. Then S is countable.

theorem.countable-union-countable.notes: Theorem 2.12 in Rudin. A fundamental result on the closure of countable sets under countable unions.

title.en: Countable Union of Countable Sets is Countable

natural.en: Suppose f is a real differentiable function on [a, b] and suppose f'(a) < lambda < f'(b). Then there is a point x in (a, b) such that f'(x) = lambda. A similar result holds if f'(a) > f'(b).

theorem.darboux-theorem.notes: This theorem shows that derivatives, even when discontinuous, satisfy the intermediate value property. The proof considers g(t) = f(t) - lambda*t and applies the extreme value theorem (4.16) and Fermat's theorem (5.8). Rudin labels this result as Theorem 5.12; it is classically known as Darboux's theorem.

title.en: Darboux's Theorem (Intermediate Value Property of Derivatives)

natural.en: d/dx(cos⁻¹ x) = -1/√(1 - x²), for -1 < x < 1.
natural.es: d/dx(cos⁻¹ x) = -1/√(1 - x²), para -1 < x < 1.

theorem.derivative-arccos.notes: Similar to arcsin: if y = cos⁻¹ x then cos y = x, so -sin y · dy/dx = 1, giving dy/dx = -1/sin y = -1/√(1 - x²).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: d/dx(sin⁻¹ x) = 1/√(1 - x²), for -1 < x < 1.
natural.es: d/dx(sin⁻¹ x) = 1/√(1 - x²), para -1 < x < 1.

theorem.derivative-arcsin.notes: Derived via implicit differentiation: if y = sin⁻¹ x then sin y = x, so cos y · dy/dx = 1, giving dy/dx = 1/cos y = 1/√(1 - sin²y) = 1/√(1 - x²).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: d/dx(tan⁻¹ x) = 1/(1 + x²).
natural.es: d/dx(tan⁻¹ x) = 1/(1 + x²).

theorem.derivative-arctan.notes: If y = tan⁻¹ x then tan y = x, so sec²y · dy/dx = 1, giving dy/dx = 1/sec²y = 1/(1 + tan²y) = 1/(1 + x²).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: The derivative of a constant function is 0. That is, d/dx(c) = 0.
natural.es: La derivada de una función constante es 0. Es decir, d/dx(c) = 0.

theorem.derivative-constant.notes: Follows directly from the definition of the derivative: the difference quotient (f(x+h) - f(x))/h = (c - c)/h = 0 for all h.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: d/dx(cos x) = -sin x.
natural.es: d/dx(cos x) = -sin x.

theorem.derivative-cos.notes: Proved similarly to sin, using the addition formula for cosine and the same two special limits.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: d/dx(cot x) = -csc²x.
natural.es: d/dx(cot x) = -csc²x.

theorem.derivative-cot.notes: cot x = cos x / sin x. Apply the quotient rule using d/dx(sin x) = cos x and d/dx(cos x) = -sin x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: d/dx(csc x) = -csc x cot x.
natural.es: d/dx(csc x) = -csc x cot x.

theorem.derivative-csc.notes: csc x = 1/sin x. Apply the quotient rule (or reciprocal rule) using d/dx(sin x) = cos x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: e = lim(x→0) (1 + x)^{1/x}. This formula is a consequence of the derivative of ln x evaluated at x = 1.
natural.es: e = lim(x→0) (1 + x)^{1/x}. Esta fórmula es consecuencia de la derivada de ln x evaluada en x = 1.

theorem.derivative-e-formula.notes: Stewart derives this from ln'(1) = 1: lim(x→0) [ln(1+x)]/x = 1, so lim(x→0) ln(1+x)^{1/x} = 1, hence (1+x)^{1/x} → e.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.en: The number e as a limit

natural.en: d/dx(e^x) = e^x. The natural exponential function is its own derivative.
natural.es: d/dx(e^x) = e^x. La función exponencial natural es su propia derivada.

theorem.derivative-exponential.notes: Follows from the definition of e as the base for which lim(h→0)(e^h - 1)/h = 1 and the definition of the derivative.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: d/dx(a^x) = a^x ln a, for a > 0, a ≠ 1.
natural.es: d/dx(a^x) = a^x ln a, para a > 0, a ≠ 1.

theorem.derivative-general-exponential.notes: Since a^x = e^{x ln a}, apply the chain rule: d/dx(e^{x ln a}) = e^{x ln a} · ln a = a^x ln a.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.es: Derivada de la función exponencial general

natural.en: d/dx(ln x) = 1/x, for x > 0.
natural.es: d/dx(ln x) = 1/x, para x > 0.

theorem.derivative-ln.notes: Derived via implicit differentiation: if y = ln x then e^y = x, so e^y · dy/dx = 1, giving dy/dx = 1/e^y = 1/x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: d/dx(ln|x|) = 1/x, for x ≠ 0.
natural.es: d/dx(ln|x|) = 1/x, para x ≠ 0.

theorem.derivative-ln-abs.notes: For x > 0, ln|x| = ln x so d/dx = 1/x. For x < 0, ln|x| = ln(-x) so d/dx = (1/(-x))·(-1) = 1/x by the chain rule.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: d/dx(log_a x) = 1/(x ln a), for x > 0, a > 0, a ≠ 1.
natural.es: d/dx(log_a x) = 1/(x ln a), para x > 0, a > 0, a ≠ 1.

theorem.derivative-log-base-a.notes: Follows from the change of base formula log_a x = ln x / ln a and the derivative of ln x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.es: Derivada del logaritmo en base a

natural.en: d/dx(sec x) = sec x tan x.
natural.es: d/dx(sec x) = sec x tan x.

theorem.derivative-sec.notes: sec x = 1/cos x. Apply the quotient rule using d/dx(cos x) = -sin x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: d/dx(sin x) = cos x.
natural.es: d/dx(sin x) = cos x.

theorem.derivative-sin.notes: Stewart proves this from the definition of the derivative using the addition formula for sine and the special limits sin(h)/h → 1 and (cos h - 1)/h → 0.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: If f and g are defined on [a, b] and are differentiable at a point x in [a, b], then f + g is differentiable at x and (f + g)'(x) = f'(x) + g'(x).

theorem.derivative-sum-rule.notes: Rudin (5.3a) states this as part of a combined theorem with the product and quotient rules. Stewart treats the sum rule as immediate from limit laws and does not give it a separate theorem number.

natural.en: d/dx(tan x) = sec²x.
natural.es: d/dx(tan x) = sec²x.

theorem.derivative-tan.notes: tan x = sin x / cos x. Apply the quotient rule using d/dx(sin x) = cos x and d/dx(cos x) = -sin x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

theorem.differentiable-implies-continuou.latex: f \text{ diferenciable en } a \implies f \text{ continua en } a

natural.en: If f is differentiable at a, then f is continuous at a.
natural.es: Si f es diferenciable en a, entonces f es continua en a.

theorem.differentiable-implies-continuou.notes: Stewart proves this theorem in section 2.8. The converse is false: f(x) = |x| is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there. Rudin (5.2) gives the same proof using Theorem 4.4 (limit laws).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: If the partial sums A_n of Σa_n are bounded, b_0 ≥ b_1 ≥ b_2 ≥ ..., and lim b_n = 0, then Σa_n b_n converges.
If lim(n→∞) aₙ does not exist or if lim(n→∞) aₙ ≠ 0, then the series ∑ aₙ diverges.
natural.es: Si lim(n→∞) aₙ no existe o si lim(n→∞) aₙ ≠ 0, entonces la serie ∑ aₙ diverge.

theorem.divergence-test.notes: The converse is false: lim aₙ = 0 does not imply convergence (e.g., the harmonic series).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: The limit of (1 + 1/n)^n as n approaches infinity equals e.
The number e is irrational.

Suppose x, y, z ∈ R^k and α is real. Then (a) |x| ≥ 0, (b) |x| = 0 if and only if x = 0, (c) |αx| = |α||x|, (d) |x · y| ≤ |x||y| (Cauchy-Schwarz), (e) |x + y| ≤ |x| + |y| (triangle inequality), (f) |x - z| ≤ |x - y| + |y - z| (triangle inequality for distance).

theorem.euclidean-norm-properties.notes: Rudin Theorem 1.37. Parts (a), (b), (f) make R^k a metric space (see Chapter 2). Part (d) is an immediate consequence of the Schwarz inequality (Theorem 1.35).

natural.en: For every real x > 0 and every integer n > 0 there is one and only one positive real y such that y^n = x. This number y is written ⁿ√x or x^(1/n).

theorem.existence-of-nth-roots.notes: Rudin Theorem 1.21. Proof uses the LUB property: y = sup E where E = {t > 0 : t^n < x}, then shows y^n < x and y^n > x both lead to contradictions.

title.en: Existence and Uniqueness of nth Roots

natural.en: There exists an ordered field R which has the least-upper-bound property. Moreover, R contains Q as a subfield.

theorem.existence-of-reals.notes: Rudin Theorem 1.19. The core existence theorem of Chapter 1. Proof via Dedekind cuts is given in the Appendix (Steps 1-9). Any two ordered fields with the LUB property are isomorphic.

natural.en: If f is continuous on a closed interval [a, b], then f attains an absolute maximum value f(c) and an absolute minimum value f(d) at some numbers c and d in [a, b].
natural.es: Si f es continua en un intervalo cerrado [a, b], entonces f alcanza un valor máximo absoluto f(c) y un valor mínimo absoluto f(d) en algún par de números c y d en [a, b].

theorem.extreme-value-theorem.notes: Stewart states this theorem without proof. The proof requires the completeness of the real numbers (Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem or equivalent). It depends on continuity on a closed interval.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

theorem.extreme-value-theorem-compact-me.latex:
f : X \to \mathbb{R} \text{ continuous},\; X \text{ compact}
\;\Rightarrow\; \exists\, p,q \in X : f(p) = \sup f,\; f(q) = \inf f

natural.en: Suppose f is a continuous real function on a compact metric space X, and M = sup_{p∈X} f(p), m = inf_{p∈X} f(p). Then there exist points p, q ∈ X such that f(p) = M and f(q) = m.

theorem.extreme-value-theorem-compact-me.notes: Strictly more general than Stewart's theorem.extreme-value-theorem which is restricted to continuous functions on [a,b] ⊂ R. In R with the standard topology, [a,b] is compact (Heine-Borel), so Stewart's version is a special case.

theorem.fermat-theorem.latex:
f \text{ has local extremum at } c \;\wedge\; f'(c) \text{ exists}
\;\Rightarrow\; f'(c) = 0

natural.en: If f has a local maximum or minimum at c, and f'(c) exists, then f'(c) = 0.
natural.es: Si f tiene un máximo o mínimo local en c y f'(c) existe, entonces f'(c) = 0.

theorem.fermat-theorem.notes: Stewart proves this by analyzing one-sided limits of the difference quotient at a local maximum. Rudin (5.8) gives the same proof: left-hand quotient >= 0 and right-hand quotient <= 0 force f'(x) = 0. The key lemma for the Mean Value Theorem.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: If {Kα} is a collection of compact subsets of a metric space such that every finite subcollection has nonempty intersection, then ⋂ Kα is nonempty.

theorem.finite-intersection-compact.notes: Theorem 2.36 in Rudin. The finite intersection property characterization of compactness.

title.en: Finite Intersection Property for Compact Sets

natural.en: Suppose f is bounded on [a, b], f has only finitely many points of discontinuity on [a, b], and alpha is continuous at every point at which f is discontinuous. Then f is in R(alpha).

theorem.finitely-discontinuous-integrabl.notes: If f and alpha share a common point of discontinuity, f need not be in R(alpha). See Rudin Exercise 3.

title.en: Bounded Functions with Finitely Many Discontinuities are Integrable

natural.en: If f is continuous on [a, b], then the function g defined by g(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt, for a ≤ x ≤ b, is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), and g'(x) = f(x).
natural.es: Si f es continua en [a, b], entonces la función g definida por g(x) = ∫_a^x f(t) dt, con a ≤ x ≤ b, es continua en [a, b] y derivable en (a, b), y g'(x) = f(x).

theorem.ftc-part1.notes: FTC Part 1 establishes that differentiation and integration are inverse processes. It says that every continuous function has an antiderivative, and provides a way to construct it.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.en: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 1

natural.en: If f is continuous on [a, b], then ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f, that is, a function such that F' = f.
natural.es: Si f es continua en [a, b], entonces ∫_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a), donde F es cualquier antiderivada de f, es decir, una función tal que F' = f.

theorem.ftc-part2.notes: FTC Part 2 (the Evaluation Theorem) provides the practical method for computing definite integrals. Stewart often writes F(b) - F(a) = F(x)|_a^b = [F(x)]_a^b.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.en: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, Part 2

natural.en: If f and F map [a, b] into R^k, if f in R on [a, b], and if F' = f, then integral_a^b f(t) dt = F(b) - F(a).

title.en: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus for Vector-Valued Functions

theorem.fundamental-theorem-of-calculus.latex:
f \in \mathscr{R},\; F' = f \text{ on } [a,b]
\implies \int_a^b f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)

natural.en: If f is in R on [a, b] and if there is a differentiable function F on [a, b] such that F' = f, then integral_a^b f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a).

theorem.fundamental-theorem-of-calculus.notes: Strictly more general than Stewart's FTC Part 2 (theorem.ftc-part2): Rudin requires only f in R and existence of F with F' = f, without requiring f to be continuous. Stewart's version assumes continuity of f (which guarantees both integrability and existence of antiderivative).

natural.en: If F is an antiderivative of f on an interval I, then the most general antiderivative of f on I is F(x) + C, where C is an arbitrary constant.
natural.es: Si F es una antiderivada de f en un intervalo I, entonces la antiderivada más general de f en I es F(x) + C, donde C es una constante arbitraria.

theorem.general-antiderivative.notes: Direct consequence of the corollary that functions with equal derivatives differ by a constant.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: If f and g are continuous real functions on [a, b] which are differentiable in (a, b), then there is a point x in (a, b) at which [f(b) - f(a)]g'(x) = [g(b) - g(a)]f'(x).

theorem.generalized-mean-value-theorem.notes: Also known as Cauchy's mean value theorem. Rudin derives the ordinary MVT (5.10) as the special case g(x) = x. The proof constructs h(t) = [f(b)-f(a)]g(t) - [g(b)-g(a)]f(t), shows h(a) = h(b), and applies the extreme value theorem (4.16) and Fermat's theorem (5.8) to find x where h'(x) = 0. This theorem is the key tool for proving L'Hospital's rule (5.13).

natural.en: The geometric series ∑_{n=1}^∞ arⁿ⁻¹ = a + ar + ar² + ... converges if |r| < 1 and its sum is a/(1-r). If |r| ≥ 1, the series diverges.
natural.es: La serie geométrica ∑_{n=1}^∞ arⁿ⁻¹ = a + ar + ar² + ... converge si |r| < 1 y su suma es a/(1-r). Si |r| ≥ 1, la serie diverge.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: A set E in Rk has one of the following properties iff it has all three: (a) E is closed and bounded, (b) E is compact, (c) every infinite subset of E has a limit point in E.

theorem.heine-borel.notes: Theorem 2.41 in Rudin. The Heine-Borel theorem characterizing compact subsets of Euclidean space.

theorem.indefinite-integral-differentiab.latex:
F(x) = \int_a^x f(t)\,dt \implies F \in C[a,b]; \quad
f \text{ continuous at } x_0 \implies F'(x_0) = f(x_0)

natural.en: Let f in R on [a, b]. For a <= x <= b, put F(x) = integral_a^x f(t) dt. Then F is continuous on [a, b]; furthermore, if f is continuous at a point x_0 of [a, b], then F is differentiable at x_0 and F'(x_0) = f(x_0).

theorem.indefinite-integral-differentiab.notes: Strictly more general than Stewart's FTC Part 1 (theorem.ftc-part1): Rudin only requires f in R (not necessarily continuous everywhere), proves F continuous always, and F'(x_0) = f(x_0) only at continuity points of f. Stewart requires f continuous on all of [a,b].

title.en: Continuity and Differentiability of the Indefinite Integral

natural.en: If E is an infinite subset of a compact set K, then E has a limit point in K.

theorem.infinite-subset-compact-limit-po.notes: Theorem 2.37 in Rudin. Proved by contradiction using open covers.

title.en: Infinite Subset of a Compact Set Has a Limit Point

natural.en: If f is continuous on [a, b], or if f has only a finite number of jump discontinuities, then f is integrable on [a, b]; that is, the definite integral ∫_a^b f(x)dx exists.
natural.es: Si f es continua en [a, b], o si f tiene sólo un número finito de discontinuidades de salto, entonces f es integrable en [a, b]; es decir, la integral definida ∫_a^b f(x)dx existe.

theorem.integrability-of-continuous-func.notes: Stewart states this without proof. A rigorous proof requires the uniform continuity theorem (which follows from the completeness of the reals).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: Suppose f is a continuous, positive, decreasing function on [1, ∞) and let aₙ = f(n). Then the series ∑_{n=1}^∞ aₙ converges if and only if the improper integral ∫_1^∞ f(x) dx converges.
natural.es: Suponga que f es una función continua, positiva y decreciente en [1, ∞) y sea aₙ = f(n). Entonces la serie ∑_{n=1}^∞ aₙ converge si y sólo si la integral impropia ∫_1^∞ f(x) dx converge.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: If f maps [a, b] into R^k and f in R(alpha) for some monotonically increasing alpha on [a, b], then |f| in R(alpha) and |integral_a^b f d alpha| <= integral_a^b |f| d alpha.
If f and g are differentiable, then ∫ f(x)g'(x) dx = f(x)g(x) - ∫ g(x)f'(x) dx. Using the notation u = f(x), v = g(x): ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du.
natural.es: Si f y g son diferenciables, entonces ∫ f(x)g'(x) dx = f(x)g(x) - ∫ g(x)f'(x) dx. Con la notación u = f(x), v = g(x): ∫ u dv = uv - ∫ v du.

theorem.integration-by-parts.notes: The integration counterpart of the product rule. Stewart derives it by integrating both sides of the product rule and rearranging.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: If f and g are differentiable and their derivatives are continuous on [a, b], then ∫_a^b f(x)g'(x) dx = [f(x)g(x)]_a^b - ∫_a^b g(x)f'(x) dx.
natural.es: Si f y g son diferenciables y sus derivadas son continuas en [a, b], entonces ∫_a^b f(x)g'(x) dx = [f(x)g(x)]_a^b - ∫_a^b g(x)f'(x) dx.

theorem.integration-by-parts-definite.notes: The definite integral version of integration by parts. Follows from applying FTC Part 2 to the indefinite integration by parts formula.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.en: Integration by Parts for Definite Integrals
title.es: Integración por partes para integrales definidas

natural.en: Suppose F and G are differentiable functions on [a, b], F' = f in R, and G' = g in R. Then integral_a^b F(x) g(x) dx = F(b)G(b) - F(a)G(a) - integral_a^b f(x) G(x) dx.

theorem.integration-by-parts-riemann.notes: Rudin's version requires only F', G' in R (integrable), not necessarily continuous. Stewart's integration-by-parts-definite typically requires continuous derivatives.

theorem.integration-step-function.latex:
\alpha(x) = I(x - s),\; f \text{ continuous at } s
\implies \int_a^b f\,d\alpha = f(s)

natural.en: If a < s < b, f is bounded on [a, b], f is continuous at s, and alpha(x) = I(x - s) (the unit step at s), then integral_a^b f d alpha = f(s).

title.en: Integration with Respect to a Step Function

theorem.integration-step-series.latex:
\alpha(x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} c_n I(x - s_n)
\implies
\int_a^b f\,d\alpha = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} c_n f(s_n)

natural.en: Suppose c_n >= 0 for n = 1, 2, 3, ..., sum c_n converges, {s_n} is a sequence of distinct points in (a, b), and alpha(x) = sum c_n I(x - s_n). Let f be continuous on [a, b]. Then integral_a^b f d alpha = sum c_n f(s_n).

title.en: Integration with Respect to a Series of Step Functions

theorem.intermediate-value-theorem.latex: f \text{ continua en } [a,b], \; N \text{ entre } f(a) \text{ y } f(b) \implies \exists\, c \in (a,b) : f(c) = N

natural.en: Suppose that f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b] and let N be any number between f(a) and f(b), where f(a) ≠ f(b). Then there exists a number c in (a, b) such that f(c) = N.
natural.es: Suponga que f es continua en el intervalo cerrado [a, b] y sea N cualquier número entre f(a) y f(b), donde f(a) ≠ f(b). Entonces existe un número c en (a, b) tal que f(c) = N.

theorem.intermediate-value-theorem.notes: Stewart states the IVT without proof in section 2.5. Rudin proves it in Theorem 4.23 via the continuous image of connected sets (Thm 4.22) and the characterization of connected subsets of R (Thm 2.47).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: Every k-cell is compact.

theorem.k-cell-compact.notes: Theorem 2.40 in Rudin. Key step toward the Heine-Borel theorem.

natural.en: Suppose that f and g are differentiable and g'(x) ≠ 0 near a (except possibly at a). Suppose that lim(x→a) f(x) = 0 and lim(x→a) g(x) = 0, or that lim(x→a) f(x) = ±∞ and lim(x→a) g(x) = ±∞ (i.e., we have an indeterminate form of type 0/0 or ∞/∞). Then lim(x→a) f(x)/g(x) = lim(x→a) f'(x)/g'(x), if the limit on the right side exists (or is ±∞).
natural.es: Suponga que f y g son derivables y que g'(x) ≠ 0 cerca de a (excepto posiblemente en a). Suponga que lim(x→a) f(x) = 0 y lim(x→a) g(x) = 0, o que lim(x→a) f(x) = ±∞ y lim(x→a) g(x) = ±∞ (es decir, que se tiene una forma indeterminada 0/0 o ∞/∞). Entonces lim(x→a) f(x)/g(x) = lim(x→a) f'(x)/g'(x), si el límite del lado derecho existe (o es ±∞).

theorem.lhopitals-rule.notes: Stewart proves the 0/0 case using the Cauchy Mean Value Theorem (a generalization of MVT). The ∞/∞ case is stated without complete proof. The rule also applies to one-sided limits and limits at infinity. Rudin (5.13) proves both the 0/0 and ∞/∞ cases rigorously using the generalized MVT (5.9), and allows -∞ <= a < b <= +∞ (extended reals).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: Let f and g be defined on E. Suppose f(t) → A and g(t) → B as t → x (in the extended real number system). Then (a) f(t) → A' implies A' = A (uniqueness); (b) (f+g)(t) → A + B; (c) (fg)(t) → AB; (d) (f/g)(t) → A/B, provided the right members are defined.

theorem.limit-arithmetic-extended-real.notes: The expressions ∞ − ∞, 0·∞, ∞/∞, A/0 are not defined. Proof is analogous to Theorem 4.4.

title.en: Arithmetic of Limits in the Extended Real Number System

natural.en: Suppose E ⊂ X (a metric space), p is a limit point of E, f and g are complex functions on E, and lim_{x→p} f(x) = A, lim_{x→p} g(x) = B. Then (a) lim_{x→p}(f+g)(x) = A + B; (b) lim_{x→p}(fg)(x) = AB; (c) lim_{x→p}(f/g)(x) = A/B if B ≠ 0.
Suppose ∑ aₙ and ∑ bₙ are series with positive terms. If lim(n→∞) aₙ/bₙ = c, where c is a finite number and c > 0, then either both series converge or both diverge.
natural.es: Suponga que ∑ aₙ y ∑ bₙ son series con términos positivos. Si lim(n→∞) aₙ/bₙ = c, donde c es un número finito y c > 0, entonces ambas series convergen o ambas divergen.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.es: Prueba de comparación en el límite

theorem.limit-laws.latex:
\begin{aligned}
&\lim_{x \to a} [f(x) + g(x)] = \lim_{x \to a} f(x) + \lim_{x \to a} g(x) \\
&\lim_{x \to a} [f(x) - g(x)] = \lim_{x \to a} f(x) - \lim_{x \to a} g(x) \\
&\lim_{x \to a} [c \cdot f(x)] = c \cdot \lim_{x \to a} f(x) \\
&\lim_{x \to a} [f(x) \cdot g(x)] = \lim_{x \to a} f(x) \cdot \lim_{x \to a} g(x) \\
&\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{\lim_{x \to a} f(x)}{\lim_{x \to a} g(x)} \quad \text{si } \lim_{x \to a} g(x) \neq 0
\end{aligned}

natural.en: Suppose that c is a constant and the limits lim(x→a) f(x) and lim(x→a) g(x) exist. Then: 1. lim(x→a) [f(x) + g(x)] = lim(x→a) f(x) + lim(x→a) g(x), 2. lim(x→a) [f(x) - g(x)] = lim(x→a) f(x) - lim(x→a) g(x), 3. lim(x→a) [cf(x)] = c lim(x→a) f(x), 4. lim(x→a) [f(x)g(x)] = lim(x→a) f(x) · lim(x→a) g(x), 5. lim(x→a) [f(x)/g(x)] = lim(x→a) f(x) / lim(x→a) g(x), provided lim(x→a) g(x) ≠ 0.
natural.es: Suponga que c es una constante y que los límites lim(x→a) f(x) y lim(x→a) g(x) existen. Entonces: 1. lim(x→a) [f(x) + g(x)] = lim(x→a) f(x) + lim(x→a) g(x), 2. lim(x→a) [f(x) - g(x)] = lim(x→a) f(x) - lim(x→a) g(x), 3. lim(x→a) [cf(x)] = c lim(x→a) f(x), 4. lim(x→a) [f(x)g(x)] = lim(x→a) f(x) · lim(x→a) g(x), 5. lim(x→a) [f(x)/g(x)] = lim(x→a) f(x) / lim(x→a) g(x), si lim(x→a) g(x) ≠ 0.

theorem.limit-laws.notes: Stewart presents these as the fundamental laws for computing limits. The proofs use the epsilon-delta definition from section 2.4.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

natural.en: lim(x→∞) 1/xʳ = 0 and lim(x→-∞) 1/xʳ = 0 if r > 0 is a rational number and xʳ is defined for all x.
natural.es: lim(x→∞) 1/xʳ = 0 y lim(x→-∞) 1/xʳ = 0 si r > 0 es un número racional y xʳ está definido para todo x.

theorem.limit-one-over-x-at-infinity.notes: This is the fundamental building block for evaluating limits at infinity of rational functions by dividing numerator and denominator by the highest power of x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.en: Limit of 1/x as x approaches infinity
title.es: Límite de 1/x cuando x tiende a infinito

natural.en: If lim(x→a) f(x) exists and n is a positive integer, then lim(x→a) [f(x)]ⁿ = [lim(x→a) f(x)]ⁿ.
natural.es: Si lim(x→a) f(x) existe y n es un entero positivo, entonces lim(x→a) [f(x)]ⁿ = [lim(x→a) f(x)]ⁿ.

theorem.limit-power-law.notes: Follows from repeated application of the product law (law 4 of the limit laws).

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.es: Ley de la potencia para límites

natural.en: If lim(x→a) f(x) exists and n is a positive integer, then lim(x→a) ⁿ√f(x) = ⁿ√(lim(x→a) f(x)). If n is even, we require that lim(x→a) f(x) > 0.
natural.es: Si lim(x→a) f(x) existe y n es un entero positivo, entonces lim(x→a) ⁿ√f(x) = ⁿ√(lim(x→a) f(x)). Si n es par, se requiere que lim(x→a) f(x) > 0.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.es: Ley de la raíz para límites

natural.en: The limit of sin(x)/x as x approaches 0 equals 1.
natural.es: El límite de sen(x)/x cuando x tiende a 0 es igual a 1.

theorem.limit-sinx-over-x.notes: Stewart proves this using the squeeze theorem with a geometric argument involving areas of sectors and triangles in the unit circle. This result is essential for differentiating trigonometric functions.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.en: Limit of sin(x)/x as x approaches 0
title.es: Límite de sen(x)/x cuando x tiende a 0

natural.en: For any bounded real function f and monotonically increasing alpha on [a, b], the lower Riemann-Stieltjes integral does not exceed the upper Riemann-Stieltjes integral.

title.en: Lower Integral is at Most Upper Integral

natural.en: Suppose S is an ordered set with the least-upper-bound property, B ⊂ S, B is not empty, and B is bounded below. Let L be the set of all lower bounds of B. Then α = sup L exists in S, and α = inf B. In particular, inf B exists in S.

theorem.lub-implies-glb.notes: Rudin Theorem 1.11. Shows that the LUB property automatically gives the GLB property. A fundamental duality result.

natural.en: Suppose f is a continuous mapping of [a, b] into R^k and f is differentiable in (a, b). Then there exists x in (a, b) such that |f(b) - f(a)| <= (b - a)|f'(x)|.

theorem.mean-value-inequality-vector.notes: The mean value theorem fails for vector-valued functions (Example 5.17 shows f(x) = e^{ix} has f(2pi)-f(0) = 0 but |f'(x)| = 1). This inequality is the best substitute. The proof uses the inner product z = f(b) - f(a), reduces to a real-valued function phi(t) = z . f(t), applies the real MVT, and finishes with the Schwarz inequality. Proof due to V. P. Havin.

title.en: Mean Value Inequality for Vector-Valued Functions

natural.en: Let f be a function that satisfies the following hypotheses: 1. f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b]. 2. f is differentiable on the open interval (a, b). Then there is a number c in (a, b) such that f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a), or equivalently, f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b - a).
natural.es: Sea f una función que satisface las dos hipótesis siguientes: 1. f es continua en el intervalo cerrado [a, b]. 2. f es derivable en el intervalo abierto (a, b). Entonces existe un número c en (a, b) tal que f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a), o equivalentemente, f(b) - f(a) = f'(c)(b - a).

theorem.mean-value-theorem.notes: One of the most important theorems in calculus. Stewart proves it by applying Rolle's theorem to the auxiliary function h(x) = f(x) - [f(a) + ((f(b)-f(a))/(b-a))(x-a)]. Rudin (5.10) derives it as a corollary of the generalized mean value theorem (5.9) by taking g(x) = x.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

theorem.mean-value-theorem-integrals.latex:
\int_a^b f(x)\,dx = f(c)(b - a)
\quad\text{for some } c \in [a, b]

natural.en: If f is continuous on [a, b], then there exists a number c in [a, b] such that f(c) = f_avg = (1/(b-a)) ∫_a^b f(x) dx, that is, ∫_a^b f(x) dx = f(c)(b - a).
natural.es: Si f es continua en [a, b], entonces existe un número c en [a, b] tal que f(c) = f_prom = (1/(b-a)) ∫_a^b f(x) dx, es decir, ∫_a^b f(x) dx = f(c)(b - a).

theorem.mean-value-theorem-integrals.notes: Stewart presents this as a consequence of the Intermediate Value Theorem applied to the integral function. It guarantees the existence of a point where the function attains its average value.

sources.author: James Stewart
sources.work: Cálculo de una variable — Trascendentes tempranas

title.es: Teorema del valor medio para integrales

theorem.mertens.latex: \sum a_n = A \text{ (abs.)},\; \sum b_n = B \implies \sum c_n = AB

natural.en: If Σa_n converges absolutely to A, Σb_n = B, and c_n = Σ_{k=0}^n a_k b_{n-k}, then Σc_n = AB.

theorem.monotone-countable-discontinuiti.latex:
f \text{ monotonic on } (a,b) \;\Rightarrow\;
\{x \in (a,b) : f \text{ discontinuous at } x\} \text{ is at most countable}

natural.en: Let f be monotonic on (a, b). Then the set of points of (a, b) at which f is discontinuous is at most countable.

title.en: Monotone Functions Have at Most Countably Many Discontinuities

theorem.monotone-one-sided-limits.latex: \sup_{a < t < x} f(t) = f(x-) \leq f(x) \leq f(x+) = \inf_{x < t < b} f(t)

natural.en: Let f be monotonically increasing on (a, b). Then f(x+) and f(x−) exist at every point x of (a, b). More precisely, sup_{a<t<x} f(t) = f(x−) ≤ f(x) ≤ f(x+) = inf_{x<t<b} f(t). Furthermore, if a < x < y < b, then f(x+) ≤ f(y−).
If f is monotonic on [a, b] and alpha is continuous on [a, b], then f is in R(alpha).

title.en: Monotonic Functions with Continuous Integrator are Integrable

natural.en: Every bounded, monotonic sequence is convergent.
natural.es: Toda sucesión acotada y monótona es convergente.

theorem.monotonic-sequence-theorem.notes: Stewart states this theorem using the Completeness Axiom (least upper bound property). The proof relies on the existence of the supremum for bounded sets.

natural.en: The integral of a rate of change is the net change: ∫_a^b F'(x) dx = F(b) - F(a).
natural.es: La integral de una tasa de cambio es el cambio neto: ∫_a^b F'(x) dx = F(b) - F(a).

theorem.net-change-theorem.notes: This is a restatement of FTC Part 2 interpreted in terms of rates of change. Stewart presents it as a conceptual framework for applications (displacement, accumulated quantity, etc.).

natural.en: Let E be a noncompact set in R¹. Then (a) there exists a continuous function on E which is not bounded; (b) there exists a continuous and bounded function on E which has no maximum. If in addition E is bounded, then (c) there exists a continuous function on E which is not uniformly continuous.

theorem.noncompact-counterexamples.notes: Shows that compactness is essential in Theorems 4.14, 4.15, 4.16, and 4.19. Part (c) would be false if boundedness were omitted (e.g., every function on the integers is uniformly continuous).

title.en: Necessity of Compactness for Continuity Theorems

natural.en: Suppose Y ⊂ X. A subset E of Y is open relative to Y if and only if E = Y ∩ G for some open subset G of X.

theorem.open-relative.notes: Theorem 2.30 in Rudin. Characterizes the subspace topology via intersections.

natural.en: The series Σ1/n^p converges if p > 1 and diverges if p ≤ 1.
Let P be a nonempty perfect set in Rk. Then P is uncountable.

theorem.perfect-set-uncountable.notes: Theorem 2.43 in Rudin. Uses nested compact sets and the Baire category-style argument.

natural.en: If n is any real number, then d/dx(x^n) = nx^{n-1}.
natural.es: Si n es cualquier número real, entonces d/dx(x^n) = nx^{n-1}.

theorem.power-rule.notes: Stewart proves the case n = positive integer using the binomial theorem in section 3.1. The general case (n any real number) is proved later using logarithmic differentiation in section 3.6.

theorem.power-series-boundary.latex: R = 1,\; c_n \downarrow 0 \implies \sum c_n z^n \text{ converges for } |z|=1,\; z \neq 1

natural.en: If the radius of convergence of Σc_n z^n is 1, and c_0 ≥ c_1 ≥ c_2 ≥ ..., lim c_n = 0, then Σc_n z^n converges at every point on |z| = 1 except possibly z = 1.

For a power series ∑ cₙ(x-a)ⁿ, there are only three possibilities: (i) The series converges only when x = a. (ii) The series converges for all x. (iii) There is a positive number R such that the series converges if |x-a| < R and diverges if |x-a| > R. R is called the radius of convergence.
natural.es: Para una serie de potencias ∑ cₙ(x-a)ⁿ, sólo se da una de tres posibilidades: (i) La serie converge sólo cuando x = a. (ii) La serie converge para todo x. (iii) Existe un número positivo R tal que la serie converge si |x-a| < R y diverge si |x-a| > R. R se llama radio de convergencia.

natural.en: If the power series ∑ cₙ(x-a)ⁿ has radius of convergence R > 0, then the function f(x) = ∑_{n=0}^∞ cₙ(x-a)ⁿ is differentiable (and integrable) on (a-R, a+R) and (i) f'(x) = ∑_{n=1}^∞ n·cₙ(x-a)ⁿ⁻¹, (ii) ∫ f(x) dx = C + ∑_{n=0}^∞ cₙ(x-a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1). The radii of convergence of both series are R.
natural.es: Si la serie de potencias ∑ cₙ(x-a)ⁿ tiene radio de convergencia R > 0, entonces la función f(x) = ∑_{n=0}^∞ cₙ(x-a)ⁿ es diferenciable (e integrable) en (a-R, a+R) y (i) f'(x) = ∑_{n=1}^∞ n·cₙ(x-a)ⁿ⁻¹, (ii) ∫ f(x) dx = C + ∑_{n=0}^∞ cₙ(x-a)ⁿ⁺¹/(n+1). Los radios de convergencia de ambas series son R.

theorem.power-series-differentiation-int.notes: Stewart states this theorem and uses it extensively but defers the full proof to more advanced courses. The key result is that term-by-term differentiation and integration are valid within the interval of convergence.

natural.en: If f and g are both differentiable functions, then d/dx[f(x)g(x)] = f(x) g'(x) + g(x) f'(x).
natural.es: Si f y g son funciones diferenciables, entonces d/dx[f(x)g(x)] = f(x) g'(x) + g(x) f'(x).

theorem.product-rule.notes: Stewart proves this by adding and subtracting f(x+h)g(x) in the difference quotient. Rudin (5.3b) uses h(t)-h(x) = f(t)[g(t)-g(x)] + g(x)[f(t)-f(x)] and applies Theorem 5.2 (differentiable implies continuous) and limit laws.

natural.en: If f and g are differentiable functions, then d/dx[f(x)/g(x)] = [g(x)f'(x) - f(x)g'(x)] / [g(x)]^2.
natural.es: Si f y g son funciones diferenciables, entonces d/dx[f(x)/g(x)] = [g(x)f'(x) - f(x)g'(x)] / [g(x)]^2.

theorem.quotient-rule.notes: Stewart derives the quotient rule using a similar technique to the product rule, adding and subtracting f(x)g(x) in the numerator of the difference quotient. Rudin (5.3c) lets h = f/g and applies Theorems 4.4 and 5.2.

natural.en: (i) If lim(n→∞) |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = L < 1, then the series ∑ aₙ is absolutely convergent. (ii) If lim(n→∞) |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = L > 1 or lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = ∞, the series diverges. (iii) If L = 1, the test is inconclusive.
natural.es: (i) Si lim(n→∞) |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = L < 1, entonces la serie ∑ aₙ es absolutamente convergente. (ii) Si lim(n→∞) |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = L > 1 o lim |aₙ₊₁/aₙ| = ∞, la serie diverge. (iii) Si L = 1, la prueba no es concluyente.

natural.en: For any real numbers a and b, (a, 0) + (b, 0) = (a + b, 0) and (a, 0)(b, 0) = (ab, 0). Hence the complex numbers of the form (a, 0) have the same arithmetic properties as the corresponding real numbers a.

theorem.real-subfield-of-complex.notes: Rudin Theorem 1.26. Identifies (a, 0) with a, making R a subfield of C.

title.en: Real Numbers as Subfield of Complex Numbers

natural.en: If P* is a refinement of P, then L(P, f, alpha) <= L(P*, f, alpha) and U(P*, f, alpha) <= U(P, f, alpha).

natural.en: If Σa_n is a conditionally convergent series and -∞ ≤ α ≤ β ≤ ∞, then there exists a rearrangement Σa'_n with lim inf s'_n = α and lim sup s'_n = β.
f is in R(alpha) on [a, b] if and only if for every epsilon > 0 there exists a partition P such that U(P, f, alpha) - L(P, f, alpha) < epsilon.

theorem.riemann-stieltjes-integral-prope.latex:
\int_a^b (f_1 + f_2)\,d\alpha
= \int_a^b f_1\,d\alpha + \int_a^b f_2\,d\alpha \\
\int_a^c f\,d\alpha + \int_c^b f\,d\alpha = \int_a^b f\,d\alpha \\
\left|\int_a^b f\,d\alpha\right| \le M[\alpha(b) - \alpha(a)]

natural.en: (a) If f_1, f_2 in R(alpha) on [a, b], then f_1 + f_2 in R(alpha), cf in R(alpha) for every constant c, and the integral is linear. (b) If f_1(x) <= f_2(x) on [a, b], then integral f_1 d alpha <= integral f_2 d alpha. (c) If f in R(alpha) on [a, b] and a < c < b, then f in R(alpha) on [a, c] and [c, b], and the integral is additive over subintervals. (d) If f in R(alpha) and |f(x)| <= M, then |integral f d alpha| <= M[alpha(b) - alpha(a)]. (e) If f in R(alpha_1) and f in R(alpha_2), then f in R(alpha_1 + alpha_2) and the integral is linear in alpha.

Let f be a function that satisfies the following three hypotheses: 1. f is continuous on the closed interval [a, b]. 2. f is differentiable on the open interval (a, b). 3. f(a) = f(b). Then there is a number c in (a, b) such that f'(c) = 0.
natural.es: Sea f una función que satisface las tres hipótesis siguientes: 1. f es continua en el intervalo cerrado [a, b]. 2. f es derivable en el intervalo abierto (a, b). 3. f(a) = f(b). Entonces existe un número c en (a, b) tal que f'(c) = 0.

natural.en: Let X, Y be metric spaces, E ⊂ X, f: E → Y, and p a limit point of E. Then lim_{x→p} f(x) = q if and only if lim_{n→∞} f(p_n) = q for every sequence {p_n} in E such that p_n ≠ p and lim_{n→∞} p_n = p.

theorem.squeeze-theorem.latex: f(x) \leq g(x) \leq h(x) \;\text{ and }\; \lim_{x \to a} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a} h(x) = L \implies \lim_{x \to a} g(x) = L

natural.en: If f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ h(x) when x is near a (except possibly at a) and lim(x→a) f(x) = lim(x→a) h(x) = L, then lim(x→a) g(x) = L.
natural.es: Si f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ h(x) cuando x está cerca de a (excepto posiblemente en a) y lim(x→a) f(x) = lim(x→a) h(x) = L, entonces lim(x→a) g(x) = L.

theorem.squeeze-theorem.notes: Also known as the sandwich theorem or pinching theorem. Stewart uses it to prove lim(x→0) sin(x)/x = 1.

natural.en: Assume alpha increases monotonically and alpha' is in R on [a, b]. Let f be a bounded real function on [a, b]. Then f in R(alpha) if and only if f alpha' in R. In that case, integral_a^b f d alpha = integral_a^b f(x) alpha'(x) dx.

theorem.stieltjes-riemann-reduction.notes: This theorem shows how the Stieltjes integral reduces to a Riemann integral when the integrator has an integrable derivative. Combined with Theorem 6.16, it demonstrates the unifying power of the Stieltjes formulation.

title.en: Reduction of Stieltjes Integral to Riemann Integral

natural.en: (a) If {p_n} is a sequence in a compact metric space X, then some subsequence of {p_n} converges to a point of X. (b) Every bounded sequence in R^k contains a convergent subsequence (Bolzano-Weierstrass).

theorem.subsequence-compact.notes: Theorem 3.6 from Rudin. Part (b) is the Bolzano-Weierstrass theorem, which follows from (a) since closed bounded subsets of R^k are compact by Heine-Borel.

theorem.subsequential-limits-closed.latex: E^* = \{ x : p_{n_k} \to x \text{ for some subsequence}\} \text{ is closed}

natural.en: Let {p_n} be a sequence in a metric space X. The set E* of all subsequential limits of {p_n} is a closed subset of X.

title.en: Subsequential Limits Form a Closed Set

natural.en: If u = g(x) is a differentiable function whose range is an interval I and f is continuous on I, then ∫ f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du.
natural.es: Si u = g(x) es una función derivable cuyo rango es un intervalo I y f es continua en I, entonces ∫ f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = ∫ f(u) du.

theorem.substitution-rule.notes: The substitution rule is the integration counterpart of the chain rule. It works by reversing the chain rule for derivatives.

natural.en: If g' is continuous on [a, b] and f is continuous on the range of u = g(x), then ∫_a^b f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u) du.
natural.es: Si g' es continua en [a, b] y f es continua en el rango de u = g(x), entonces ∫_a^b f(g(x)) g'(x) dx = ∫_{g(a)}^{g(b)} f(u) du.

theorem.substitution-rule-definite.notes: When using substitution in definite integrals, the limits of integration change from x-values to u-values.

natural.es: Si f y g son funciones diferenciables, entonces d/dx[f(x) + g(x)] = d/dx f(x) + d/dx g(x).

theorem.summation-by-parts.latex: \sum_{n=p}^{q} a_n b_n = \sum_{n=p}^{q-1} A_n(b_n - b_{n+1}) + A_q b_q - A_{p-1} b_p

natural.en: Given sequences {a_n} and {b_n}, put A_n = Σ_{k=0}^n a_k. Then Σ_{n=p}^q a_n b_n = Σ_{n=p}^{q-1} A_n(b_n - b_{n+1}) + A_q b_q - A_{p-1} b_p.

If f(x) = Tₙ(x) + Rₙ(x), where Tₙ is the nth-degree Taylor polynomial and Rₙ is the remainder, then if lim(n→∞) Rₙ(x) = 0 for |x-a| < R, we have f(x) = ∑_{n=0}^∞ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n! · (x-a)ⁿ. By Taylor's inequality, if |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(x)| ≤ M for |x-a| ≤ d, then |Rₙ(x)| ≤ M·dⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)!.
natural.es: Si f(x) = Tₙ(x) + Rₙ(x), donde Tₙ es el polinomio de Taylor de grado n y Rₙ es el residuo, entonces si lim(n→∞) Rₙ(x) = 0 para |x-a| < R, se tiene f(x) = ∑_{n=0}^∞ f⁽ⁿ⁾(a)/n! · (x-a)ⁿ. Por la desigualdad de Taylor, si |f⁽ⁿ⁺¹⁾(x)| ≤ M para |x-a| ≤ d, entonces |Rₙ(x)| ≤ M·dⁿ⁺¹/(n+1)!.

theorem.taylor-convergence.notes: Taylor's inequality follows from the Lagrange form of the remainder in Taylor's theorem, which itself uses the MVT.

natural.en: Suppose f is a real function on [a, b], n is a positive integer, f^(n-1) is continuous on [a, b], f^(n)(t) exists for every t in (a, b). Let alpha, beta be distinct points of [a, b], and define P(t) = sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f^(k)(alpha)/k! * (t - alpha)^k. Then there exists a point x between alpha and beta such that f(beta) = P(beta) + f^(n)(x)/n! * (beta - alpha)^n.

theorem.taylor-theorem.notes: For n = 1 this reduces to the mean value theorem. The theorem shows that f can be approximated by a polynomial of degree n-1, with the Lagrange remainder f^(n)(x)/n! * (beta - alpha)^n providing an error estimate. Different from Taylor series convergence (which concerns infinite series); this is a finite approximation result.

natural.en: (a) Arbitrary unions of open sets are open. (b) Arbitrary intersections of closed sets are closed. (c) Finite intersections of open sets are open. (d) Finite unions of closed sets are closed.

theorem.unions-intersections-open-closed.notes: Theorem 2.24 in Rudin. Four-part result on stability of open and closed sets under set operations.
